{{Japanese Imperial Rituals}}'''Shihohai''' [[Ritual|is a ritual]] in which [[Emperor of Japan|the Emperor]] pays homage to the gods of the four directions in the Imperial Palace gardens early in the morning on [[January 1|January 1st]] ( [[New Year's Day]] ) every year. This is an imperial ritual in which people bow in all four directions and pray for the elimination of annual disasters and for a bountiful harvest . {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}}
Shihohai is the name of ceremony held at Imperial Palace in the beginning of the year.
The {{ill|Shihōhai|ja|四方拝}} (Shihōhai) is a ritual performed by the Emperor at dawn on January 1st (New Year's Day), prior to the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}} (New Year's ceremony). It takes place in the south garden of the {{ill|Jingū Kaikan|ja|神嘉殿}} within the Imperial Palace, where the Emperor pays homage to the deities of heaven and earth in all directions. The ceremony is held outdoors, symbolizing the Emperor's descent to the earth to pay respect to the heavenly and earthly deities, referred to as "Tegami-no-Mi" or descending to the garden.
From the early Meiji era, when national holidays were officially designated, until around 1945, January 1st was known as "Shihō no Setsu." Article 23 of the Imperial Household Ceremonial Code (Meiji 41, Imperial Household Ordinance No. 1) stipulated that the Shihōhai should be performed before the Saitan-sai on New Year's Day, except during the Emperor's mourning period or other exceptional circumstances. After this ordinance was abolished in 1947, the ritual continued as a private event in the Imperial family according to former practices.
The gist of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year's Day), the Emperor dons a formal [[Sokutai|robe]] called [[:ja:黄櫨染御袍|']]{{ill|kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}' and enters a temporary building set up in the garden to the south of [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Shinkaden]], which is located to the west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|en}}, and bows toward both the Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu shrines of [[Ise Grand Shrine]], then makes bows to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor worships at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Shrine, the {{Ill|Amatsukami|lt=gods of heaven|en}} and {{Ill|Kunitsukami|lt=earth|en}}, the tomb [[Emperor Jimmu|of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors {{NoteTag|[[上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|上皇]][[明仁]]の場合、曾祖父・[[明治天皇]]の[[伏見桃山陵]]、祖父・[[大正天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|多摩陵]]、父・[[昭和天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|武蔵野陵]]の三陵。}}, the [[Ichinomiya|Ichinomiyas]] of many provinces: [[Musashi Province]] ( {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|lt=Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|en}}), [[Yamashiro Province]] ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine]] , [[Atsuta Shrine]], [[Hitachi Province|the Ichinomiya of Hitachi]] [[Ichinomiya|Province]] ( [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima Shrine]] ), and the Ichinomiya of [[Shimōsa Province|Shimousa Province]] ( {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮}} ).
== overview == Shihohai is a ritual in which the Emperor pays respects to the gods of the four directions of heaven and earth in the southern garden of the Shinkaden Hall in the Imperial Palace early in the morning on January 1st (New Year's Day ) every year, prior to the New Year's Festival. The reason why the ceremony is held in the garden rather than on the palace grounds is said to signify that the Emperor himself descends to earth, abdicates and bows down to the gods of heaven and earth, and this is referred to as the " '''Teijo-no-uego''' " ceremony {{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966}} .
From the early Meiji period, when the holiday was legally established, until around [[1945]] (Showa 20), January 1st, the day when this [[:ja:宮中祭祀|Imperial Court ritual]] was held, was called '''Shiho-setsu''' . Article 23 of the [[:ja:皇室祭祀令|Imperial Household Rites Order]] (Imperial Household Order No. 1 of 1908), one of the Imperial Household Ordinances, stipulates that "On the day of the New Year's Ceremony, a ceremony of worship in all four directions shall be held first...However, if the Emperor passes away or there are other circumstances, the ceremony of worship in all four directions shall not be held." After the order was abolished in [[1947]], the New Year's Ceremony has been held in accordance with the old rules as a private event of [[Imperial House of Japan|the Imperial Household]] .
The Shihohai in [[2009]] (Heisei 21) was held at the Imperial Palace due to the simplification of the rituals following the aging of the then Emperor [[Akihito]] (the 125th Emperor).
== Overview == During the early Heian period, this ceremony originated in the Imperial Palace and spread to lords and ordinary people as a wish to be in full harvest and a perfect state of health by praying in various directions no matter what the year might bring, but as time went by the ceremony remained simply as a court function.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Yu|first=A. C.|title=Shihohai - Japanese Wiki Corpus|url=https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Shihohai.html|access-date=2024-04-15|website=www.japanesewiki.com}}</ref>
== The origin of Shihohai == There are different theories that it originated in the Way of Yin and Yang or it came from China, but there are no written materials to show the exact history of how it started.<ref name=":0" />
It is believed to be true that Shihohai is a cultural ceremony that came from China and was changed to suit the Japanese culture while retaining various aspects of Chinese culture, since the Way of Yin and Yan originally came from China and has been systematized, including Chinese studies, thinking, magic and rituals.<ref name=":0" />
== History ==
=== Asuka Period: === The first documented instance of Shihōhai is mentioned in the "Nihon Shoki" during the reign of Empress Kōgyoku, describing the Emperor praying and gazing heavenward in all directions. This indicates that the ritual originated as a rain prayer during this time. The Shihōhai may have influenced the subsequent formal rituals of the Heian period.
=== Heian Period: === The formalization of Shihōhai during the Heian period is believed to have been influenced by the suburban sacrifices (Jiao sacrifices) of ancient Chinese emperors. Emperor Saga initiated the ceremony in the early Heian period at the Imperial Court. It was standardized during the reign of Emperor Uda with the earliest recorded ceremony conducted in 890 AD, according to the "Uda Tennō ki."
Azuchi-Momoyama Period: During Toyotomi Hideyoshi's rule, Onmyōji faced suppression, which disrupted traditional practices and led to the loss of significant ritual tools and texts, even for leading families such as the Tsuchimikado. The most significant rites of Onmyōdō, like the {{ill|Taizan Fukun Festival|ja|泰山府君祭}}, suffered greatly. Under the shogunate's authority, Onmyōdō was gradually integrated with Shinto practices through figures like Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by Tachikata Shintō, reforming it into {{ill|Shrine Shinto|ja|神社神道}}.
=== Before the Meiji Era: === Retired emperors during the cloistered rule performed Shihōhai, reflecting its importance in both imperial and religious contexts of Japan.
During other imperial ceremonies, regents or officials might perform rituals on behalf of the Emperor, but Shihōhai was always performed personally by the Emperor as it involved paying homage to protective stars and ancestral spirits, aligning with its origins in Daoism and Onmyōdō rather than Shinto.
In time, the practice of Shihōhai spread beyond the Imperial family, with nobles and commoners performing it for a prosperous and healthy year. However, over the centuries, it remained primarily a court ceremony.
=== Meiji Era and Later === Before Meiji: The ceremony on January 1 involved the Emperor wearing a kōrozen no gohō, performing rituals in the Imperial Palace's eastern garden at designated ritual sites. These rituals included paying respects to the Emperor's guardian stars, the deities of all directions, and ancestral tombs.
Post-Meiji: From the Meiji period onward, the influence of Daoism and related esoteric practices was removed, and Shihōhai was reconstructed as a purely Shinto ritual and incorporated into national ceremonies, becoming known as one of the four major seasonal festivals.
== History ==
=== Before the Meiji Period === It is said that the ceremony started in Emperor Saga's reign, but it was established in Emperor Uda's reign as an official ceremony, the oldest record of Shihohai being held on January 1, Kampyo 2, was in "Uda tenno gyoki" (the diary of the Emperor Uda).<ref name=":0" />
Subsequently, although the ceremony was interrupted with the [[Ōnin War|Onin War]], it started again in 1475, running from the reign of Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado to that of Emperor Komei; the ceremony was held in the front garden of the Palace of Heian (currently Kyoto Imperial Palace), Seiryo-den.<ref name=":0" />
On January 1, torano koku (at about four o'clock in the morning), the Emperor, wearing Korozen no go-ho at Ryoki-den, came to the east garden of Seiryo-den and prayed for his Zokusho (one of the stars of the Big Dipper, which is said to have destiny depending on the year in which the person was born) and spirits in every direction, or the direction of his parents' [https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Imperial%20Mausoleum.html Imperial Mausoleum], whereupon he wished for the peace and security of the nation and good harvests for the coming year.<ref name=":0" />
The chanting words on this ceremony are described in '[https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Dairi%20(the%20Imperial%20palace).html Dairi] [https://www.japanesewiki.com/history/Gishiki%20(Book).html Gishiki]' and 'Go-ke Shidai.'<ref name=":0" />
According to these materials, it is mentioned as Zokuko shichu kado ga shin, Dokuma shichu kado ga shin, Kiyaku shichu kado ga shin, Goki rokugai shichu kado ga shin, Hyakubyo joyu, Shoyoku zuishin, Kyukyu nyoritsu ryo.<ref name=":0" />
=== After the Meiji Period === After the Meiji period, it was regulated by Ordinance No. 1 of Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household), Koshitu Saishi Rei (Imperial Household Religious Rites) (1908). Prior to World War I, it was called Shiho-setsu and was conducted as a national ceremony, being considered one of the biggest of four major ceremonies held on national public holidays.<ref name=":0" />
After the war, the ceremony was continued along with Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household) ordinance, although this law was eventually abolished.<ref name=":0" />
After the war, the ceremony's name was changed to 'Shihohai' and it was conducted as a private function of the Imperial Family.<ref name=":0" />
On January 1, at about 5:30 in the morning, the Emperor, wearing a traditional formal court dress called Korozen no go-ho, would enter a building constructed in the southern garden of Shinka-den, which is located west of the Three Shrines in the Imperial Court, whereupon he would bow toward the direction of two shrines--Ko-tai jingu Shrine and Toyouke Dai-jingu Shrine of Ise-jingu Shrine--and pray to spirits in various directions.<ref name=":0" />
The Imperial mausoleums and Gods the Emperor prays for are, the Ise-jingu Shrine, Tenjin Chigi/all gods, Emperor Jimmu, former three Emperor's mausoleum (Fushimi Momoyama Imperial Mausoleum of Emperor Meiji, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Taisho, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Showa), Ichi no miya Shrine in Musashi Province (Hikawa-jinja Shrine), Ichi no miya Shrine in Yamashiro Province (Kamowake ikazuchi-jinja Shrine and Kamo mioya-jinja Shrine), Iwashimizu Hachimangu Shrine, Atsuta-jingu Shrine, Kashima-jingu Shrine and Katori-jingu Shrine.<ref name=":0" />
== History ==
=== From the early days to the end of the Edo period ===
=== Asuka Period === The first recorded documented instance of the four-way worship in Japan was in the “Nihon Shoki” ( [[Nihon Shoki|Chronicles of Japan]] ), in the entry for the first day of August in the first year of the reign of [[Empress Kōgyoku]] . {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957}} It is said that at Minami-buchi, the Emperor “bowed in all four directions and looked up to the heavens in prayer,” and this is said to be the very beginning of the custom. {{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957}} The purpose of Empress Kogyoku's worship in all four directions at this time was to pray for [[Rain dance|rain]], but since it was the emperor's personal worship and the act was called "shihohai," it is believed to have been influenced in some way by the shihohai that was institutionalized during the Heian period. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{NoteTag|皇極天皇の漢風諡号の「皇極」と重祚した時の「斉明」は中国古典に由来するが共に「中央」や北斗七星と関連がある語である{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}。}}
In addition, the imperial tombs of the Asuka and [[Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyo]] periods were octagonal tombs, and the Takamikura in the Daigokuden Hall was also octagonal in shape, which suggests that Fujiwara-kyo was the location of rituals demonstrating control over and peace in the entire land in all directions. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} For this reason, it is said that the prohibition of vicariously worshipping may be related to the Emperor's sovereign right to worship the North Star. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
=== Heian period === The establishment of the Shihohai system during the Heian period is said to have been influenced by the ancient Chinese imperial rituals known as suburban worship, which were performed by [[Emperor Kanmu]] . This was supposedly done with the support of the Baekje king, who was the only person on the Korean peninsula who performed the suburban rites to worship heaven, which had been performed by the ancient Chinese emperors (the vassal states of Silla and Goguryeo did not perform suburban rites out of respect for the emperor) through the Baekje royal family . {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}}
The current Shihohai ritual is said to have begun at the Imperial Court during the reign of [[Emperor Saga]] in the early [[Heian period]] (early [[9th century]] ). It is believed that the ritual was established during the reign of Emperor Uda (late 9th century), and the oldest record of Shihohai being performed is on [[Kanpyō (era)|New Year]] 's Day of the second year of Kanpyo (January 25, [[890]] in [[Julian calendar|the Julian]] calendar), as recorded in the " Uda Tenno Goki ."
Emperor Uda wrote, "Our country is a divine country. Therefore, every morning I pay homage to the large, medium and small deities in the four directions. This begins from now. From now on I will not neglect it even for a single day" (Uda Tenno Goki, entry for October 19, 4th year of the Ninna era). It is believed that the institution of this "daily morning worship" was founded on the premise of the "New Year's Day worship in all four directions" established during the Kōnin era of {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}} .
Disasters such as [[disease]], epidemics, [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], fires, and [[Natural disaster|natural]] disasters were all believed to be caused by the curse of [[Deity|the gods]], and [[Deity|the gods]] who caused the curses were likened to [[Oni (folklore)|demons]] or feared as gods of plague . {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007}} {{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005}} Onmyodo was developed as a form of magic based on the aristocratic society of the Heian period, and many of [[神祇祭祀|the Shinto rituals]] under the Ritsuryo system included yin and yang elements {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} . Various rituals were performed, such as [[疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God]], [[鎮花祭|the Festival for the Chinka Flower]], the Festival [[風神祭|for the Wind God]], the {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|lt=Great Purification|en}}, the Festival for the Plague God [[宮城四隅疫神祭|in the Four Corners of the Palace]], [[防解火災祭|the Firefly]] [[螢惑星祭|Planet Festival]], {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} and the Kyoto area was barrier-bound (secular and sacred areas) and rituals for the "four corners and four boundaries" such as the [[京城四隅疫神祭|Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (capital) and [[宮城四隅疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (imperial palace) were performed to pray for peace and prosperity in the world {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} .
=== Azuchi-Momoyama period === The persecution and oppression of Onmyōji (practitioners of Japanese esoteric cosmology) by Toyotomi Hideyoshi began, driving those who made a living from prayers and divinations to the provinces, and they rapidly lost power. The number of people who called themselves Onmyōji across the country far exceeded the number of official Onmyōji present in the Onmyōryo (Bureau of Yin-Yang) at the time. During the persecutions of the Sengoku period, even the leading Tsuchimikado family, lost many of their inherited Onmyōdō texts and ritual tools to fire. The most important "Great Law" of Onmyōdō, the Taizan Fukun Festival, also lost its altar, and ritual tools had to be borrowed from Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto to conduct a ground-breaking ceremony at the Imperial Palace. This had a significant impact, and the imperial rituals increasingly took on Shinto characteristics. Meanwhile, under the authorization of the shogunate, Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by the Tachikata Shintō, transformed Onmyōdō into what is known as Jinja Shintō. Before the Meiji era, retired Emperors conducting cloistered rule also occasionally performed the ritual of Shihōhai (worship in all four directions).{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}
In other bows made by the Emperor at Imperial Court ceremonies, the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|lt=regent|en}} or the head of the Shinto priest would sometimes bow on his behalf, but since the Shihohai was a bow to the Emperor's guardian star and parents, no bow was made on his behalf. In the "Kasetsu Ryakuki" written by [[白川雅喬|Masataka Shirakawa]] in the Edo period, he denies that Shihohai is a Shinto ritual, saying that it is a ritual to pay homage to guardian stars and ancestral shrines ("non-divine ritual"), so it is possible that Shihohai was a ritual established under [[Taoism]] or Onmyodo and was originally a ritual unrelated to Shinto {{Sfnp|村和明|2013}} .
Following the Emperor's example, [[Nobility|the nobles]] and commoners also performed Shihohai, praying for a good harvest and good health for the year {{NoteTag|『江家次第』には「関白四方拝」「庶臣儀」に関する記述もある{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}}, but over time it came to remain only as an Imperial Court event {{NoteTag|ただし、江戸時代においても[[摂家]]など一部の公家の間でも四方拝が行われていた記録も残されている。例えば[[元文]]3年（[[1738年]]）の元旦に当時の[[関白]][[一条兼香]]が四方拝の行った時に記録が、彼の日記『兼香公記』に残されており、それによれば、天皇の四方拝と異なり三座が設けられず、山陵に代わって[[藤原氏]]や陰陽道に関わる諸神・諸社への拝礼が行われている{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}} .
The festival was temporarily suspended during [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] in the second half of [[15th century|the 15th century]], but was revived in [[Bunmei]] 7 ( [[1475]] ) during the reign of Emperor Go- Tsuchimikado, and was held in the front garden of the Seiryoden Hall of the Kyoto Imperial Palace until the reign of [[Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Komei]] in the second half of [[19th century|the 19th century]] .
=== Ceremony before the Meiji period === At the hour of [[Tiger (zodiac)|the tiger]] on January 1st (around 4:00 a.m.), [[Emperor of Japan|the Emperor]] puts on a yellow-dyed robe at [[綾綺殿|the Ayakiden Hall]] of the Imperial Palace and appears in the east garden of Seiryoden . '''Three seats''' have already been set up in the eastern garden of Seiryoden: the Shosei Gohaigoza, the Shiho Gohaigoza, and the Yamaryo Gohaigoza.
The Emperor first sits on the "Zokusei Gohai-za" (a seat for worshipping the Emperor's star) and bows to the Emperor's assigned star {{NoteTag|属星（ぞくしょう）とは、誕生年によって定まるという人間の運命を司る[[北斗七星]]のなかの星のことで、子年は貪狼星（ドゥーベ）、丑年と亥年は巨門星（メラク）、寅年と戌年は禄存星（フェクダ）、卯年と酉年は文曲星（メグレズ）、辰年と申年は廉貞星（アリオト）、巳年と未年は武曲星（ミザール）、午年は破軍星（アルカイド、ベネトナシュ）となる<ref>{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}</ref>。}} . Next, they sit on the "Shiho Gohai-za" (four-direction worship seat) and offer prayers to the divine spirits of the four directions of heaven and earth. Finally, the person sits on the "Yama-Ryo Gohai-Oza" (pilgrimage seat) and bows in the direction of the parents' mountain tombs (omitted if the parents are still alive). Each of them prayed for the safety of the emperor and the extension of his reign. It is also known that during the Edo period, after the worship of the subordinate star, worship was made at the 'Jusei Gohaigoza' to the Naishidokoro and Ise Grand [[Ise Grand Shrine|Shrine]], and before the worship of the tombs of one's parents, worship was added to the mountain tombs of past emperors (the objects of worship varied depending on the period) at the 'Yamaryo Gohaigoza'. Regarding worship at Ise Shrine, there is an entry in the " Diary of Emperor Hanazono " [[Gen'ō|for]] January 1320 which states that this was a custom since the time of {{ill|Go-Fukakusa|lt=Emperor Go-Fukakusa|en}}, and it is believed that what was practiced by the Emperor in the Middle Ages was later adopted as the Emperor's four-way worship.
During this bow, the Emperor recited unique words (spells). According to " The Imperial Court Ceremonies " and " The Eke Ceremonies, " it is as follows.
Some historical sources refer to the "five perils" as the "five misfortunes."
Furthermore, before the Meiji period, the ritual implements used in the New Year's Day four-way worship included the " '''Great Song Folding Screen''' ," but "Great Song" referred to the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern Dynasties in China, and it has been said that the Mingtang ritual, an imperial ritual to worship heaven and earth in the Han dynasty, was inherited by Japan via the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern Dynasties. It has also been said that the yellow-dyed robe worn by the emperor in the New Year's Day four-way worship represents the earth king "yellow," who is at the center of the " monthly law " thought, and that this is related to the imperial rituals of ancient China. {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}}
According to "The Imperial Court Ceremonies" and "The Nishinomiya-ki," on New Year's Day, at the hour of the ox when the rooster crows (2:00 a.m.), four folding screens are set up in the eastern garden, and a lamp is lit in front of the seats for worshiping the divine star, and incense is burned and flowers are placed on plain wooden desks in front of each seat. The ceremony begins at the hour of the tiger (3:00 a.m.). The ritual order is as follows: 1. Worship of the affiliated star. 2. Prostration to the four directions of heaven and earth. 3. (Parents) Two worships. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
=== After the Meiji Period === After the Meiji period, from the viewpoint of {{Ill|Kokugaku|en}}, the influence of [[Taoism]] (belief in the Big Dipper and spells such as the Suiho-Ritsuryo system) was eliminated, and it was reconstructed as a Shinto ritual. It was held as a national event, called '''the Shiho-Setsu festival''', and was considered one of the four major festivals among national holidays.
; Ceremony procedure after the Meiji period : Prior to the ceremony, a temporary structure is set up in the south garden of Shinkaden, an annex to the Imperial Palace and the Three Palace Sanctuaries, with [[簾薦|a bamboo blind]] laid out in the center and two pairs of folding screens arranged around it, a throne set up within it, and two [[灯台 (照明器具)|lighthouses]] provided. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dons a yellow-dyed robe at [[綾綺殿|Ayakiden]] and is led by the Grand Master of Ceremonies out into the south garden of Shinkaden. At the worship throne, after bowing towards both the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Grand Shrines, Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu, they then bow to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor pays respects at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]], the gods of heaven and earth, [[Emperor Jimmu|the tomb of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors, [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya]] of Musashi [[Musashi Province|Province]] ( Hikawa Shrine), [[Yamashiro Province|the Ichinomiya of]] Yamashiro Province ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]] [[Atsuta Shrine|Hachiman Shrine, Atsuta Shrine]], [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya]] of Hitachi Province ( [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima Shrine]] ), and [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya of Shimousa Province]] ( Katori Shrine ), in that order. After completing the four-way worship, the Emperor pays respects at each of the three Imperial shrines (the Kashikodokoro, the Imperial Ancestors' Shrine, and the Shinto Shrine). : The custom of not performing proxy worship in the event that the Emperor has an accident and is unable to perform the four-way worship remains the same as before.
On New Year's Day in 1945, during World War II, air raid sirens sounded to warn of the impending attack of [[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|B-29 bombers]], but [[Hirohito|Emperor Showa]] used the Gobunko library, which was being used as an air raid shelter, as a makeshift funeral hall and performed a four-way worship ceremony. {{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015}}

{{Japanese Imperial Rituals}}'''Shihohai''' [[Ritual|is a ritual]] in which [[Emperor of Japan|the Emperor]] pays homage to the gods of the four directions in the Imperial Palace gardens early in the morning on [[January 1|January 1st]] ( [[New Year's Day]] ) every year. This is an imperial ritual in which people bow in all four directions and pray for the elimination of annual disasters and for a bountiful harvest . {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}}
Shihohai is the name of ceremony held at Imperial Palace in the beginning of the year.
The {{ill|Shihōhai|ja|四方拝}} (Shihōhai) is a ritual performed by the Emperor at dawn on January 1st (New Year's Day), prior to the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}} (New Year's ceremony). It takes place in the south garden of the {{ill|Jingū Kaikan|ja|神嘉殿}} within the Imperial Palace, where the Emperor pays homage to the deities of heaven and earth in all directions. The ceremony is held outdoors, symbolizing the Emperor's descent to the earth to pay respect to the heavenly and earthly deities, referred to as "Tegami-no-Mi" or descending to the garden.
From the early Meiji era, when national holidays were officially designated, until around 1945, January 1st was known as "Shihō no Setsu." Article 23 of the Imperial Household Ceremonial Code (Meiji 41, Imperial Household Ordinance No. 1) stipulated that the Shihōhai should be performed before the Saitan-sai on New Year's Day, except during the Emperor's mourning period or other exceptional circumstances. After this ordinance was abolished in 1947, the ritual continued as a private event in the Imperial family according to former practices.
The gist of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year's Day), the Emperor dons a formal [[Sokutai|robe]] called [[:ja:黄櫨染御袍|']]{{ill|kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}' and enters a temporary building set up in the garden to the south of [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Shinkaden]], which is located to the west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|en}}, and bows toward both the Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu shrines of [[Ise Grand Shrine]], then makes bows to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor worships at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Shrine, the {{Ill|Amatsukami|lt=gods of heaven|en}} and {{Ill|Kunitsukami|lt=earth|en}}, the tomb [[Emperor Jimmu|of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors {{NoteTag|[[上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|上皇]][[明仁]]の場合、曾祖父・[[明治天皇]]の[[伏見桃山陵]]、祖父・[[大正天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|多摩陵]]、父・[[昭和天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|武蔵野陵]]の三陵。}}, the [[Ichinomiya|Ichinomiyas]] of many provinces: [[Musashi Province]] ( {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|lt=Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|en}}), [[Yamashiro Province]] ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine]] , [[Atsuta Shrine]], [[Hitachi Province|the Ichinomiya of Hitachi]] [[Ichinomiya|Province]] ( [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima Shrine]] ), and the Ichinomiya of [[Shimōsa Province|Shimousa Province]] ( {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮}} ). == overview == Shihohai is a ritual in which the Emperor pays respects to the gods of the four directions of heaven and earth in the southern garden of the Shinkaden Hall in the Imperial Palace early in the morning on January 1st (New Year's Day ) every year, prior to the New Year's Festival. The reason why the ceremony is held in the garden rather than on the palace grounds is said to signify that the Emperor himself descends to earth, abdicates and bows down to the gods of heaven and earth, and this is referred to as the " '''Teijo-no-uego''' " ceremony {{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966}} .
From the early Meiji period, when the holiday was legally established, until around [[1945]] (Showa 20), January 1st, the day when this [[:ja:宮中祭祀|Imperial Court ritual]] was held, was called '''Shiho-setsu''' . Article 23 of the [[:ja:皇室祭祀令|Imperial Household Rites Order]] (Imperial Household Order No. 1 of 1908), one of the Imperial Household Ordinances, stipulates that "On the day of the New Year's Ceremony, a ceremony of worship in all four directions shall be held first...However, if the Emperor passes away or there are other circumstances, the ceremony of worship in all four directions shall not be held." After the order was abolished in [[1947]], the New Year's Ceremony has been held in accordance with the old rules as a private event of [[Imperial House of Japan|the Imperial Household]] .
The Shihohai in [[2009]] (Heisei 21) was held at the Imperial Palace due to the simplification of the rituals following the aging of the then Emperor [[Akihito]] (the 125th Emperor).
== Overview == During the early Heian period, this ceremony originated in the Imperial Palace and spread to lords and ordinary people as a wish to be in full harvest and a perfect state of health by praying in various directions no matter what the year might bring, but as time went by the ceremony remained simply as a court function.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Yu|first=A. C.|title=Shihohai - Japanese Wiki Corpus|url=https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Shihohai.html|access-date=2024-04-15|website=www.japanesewiki.com}}</ref>
== The origin of Shihohai == There are different theories that it originated in the Way of Yin and Yang or it came from China, but there are no written materials to show the exact history of how it started.<ref name=":0" />
It is believed to be true that Shihohai is a cultural ceremony that came from China and was changed to suit the Japanese culture while retaining various aspects of Chinese culture, since the Way of Yin and Yan originally came from China and has been systematized, including Chinese studies, thinking, magic and rituals.<ref name=":0" />
== History ==
=== Asuka Period: === The first documented instance of Shihōhai is mentioned in the "Nihon Shoki" during the reign of Empress Kōgyoku, describing the Emperor praying and gazing heavenward in all directions. This indicates that the ritual originated as a rain prayer during this time. The Shihōhai may have influenced the subsequent formal rituals of the Heian period.
=== Heian Period: === The formalization of Shihōhai during the Heian period is believed to have been influenced by the suburban sacrifices (Jiao sacrifices) of ancient Chinese emperors. Emperor Saga initiated the ceremony in the early Heian period at the Imperial Court. It was standardized during the reign of Emperor Uda with the earliest recorded ceremony conducted in 890 AD, according to the "Uda Tennō ki."
Azuchi-Momoyama Period: During Toyotomi Hideyoshi's rule, Onmyōji faced suppression, which disrupted traditional practices and led to the loss of significant ritual tools and texts, even for leading families such as the Tsuchimikado. The most significant rites of Onmyōdō, like the {{ill|Taizan Fukun Festival|ja|泰山府君祭}}, suffered greatly. Under the shogunate's authority, Onmyōdō was gradually integrated with Shinto practices through figures like Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by Tachikata Shintō, reforming it into {{ill|Shrine Shinto|ja|神社神道}}.
=== Before the Meiji Era: === Retired emperors during the cloistered rule performed Shihōhai, reflecting its importance in both imperial and religious contexts of Japan.
During other imperial ceremonies, regents or officials might perform rituals on behalf of the Emperor, but Shihōhai was always performed personally by the Emperor as it involved paying homage to protective stars and ancestral spirits, aligning with its origins in Daoism and Onmyōdō rather than Shinto.
In time, the practice of Shihōhai spread beyond the Imperial family, with nobles and commoners performing it for a prosperous and healthy year. However, over the centuries, it remained primarily a court ceremony.
=== Meiji Era and Later === Before Meiji: The ceremony on January 1 involved the Emperor wearing a kōrozen no gohō, performing rituals in the Imperial Palace's eastern garden at designated ritual sites. These rituals included paying respects to the Emperor's guardian stars, the deities of all directions, and ancestral tombs.
Post-Meiji: From the Meiji period onward, the influence of Daoism and related esoteric practices was removed, and Shihōhai was reconstructed as a purely Shinto ritual and incorporated into national ceremonies, becoming known as one of the four major seasonal festivals.
== History ==
=== From the early days to the end of the Edo period ===
=== Asuka Period === The first recorded documented instance of the four-way worship in Japan was in the “Nihon Shoki” ( [[Nihon Shoki|Chronicles of Japan]] ), in the entry for the first day of August in the first year of the reign of [[Empress Kōgyoku]] . {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957}} It is said that at Minami-buchi, the Emperor “bowed in all four directions and looked up to the heavens in prayer,” and this is said to be the very beginning of the custom. {{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957}} The purpose of Empress Kogyoku's worship in all four directions at this time was to pray for [[Rain dance|rain]], but since it was the emperor's personal worship and the act was called "shihohai," it is believed to have been influenced in some way by the shihohai that was institutionalized during the Heian period. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{NoteTag|皇極天皇の漢風諡号の「皇極」と重祚した時の「斉明」は中国古典に由来するが共に「中央」や北斗七星と関連がある語である{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}。}}
In addition, the imperial tombs of the Asuka and [[Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyo]] periods were octagonal tombs, and the Takamikura in the Daigokuden Hall was also octagonal in shape, which suggests that Fujiwara-kyo was the location of rituals demonstrating control over and peace in the entire land in all directions. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} For this reason, it is said that the prohibition of vicariously worshipping may be related to the Emperor's sovereign right to worship the North Star. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
=== Heian period === The establishment of the Shihohai system during the Heian period is said to have been influenced by the ancient Chinese imperial rituals known as suburban worship, which were performed by [[Emperor Kanmu]] . This was supposedly done with the support of the Baekje king, who was the only person on the Korean peninsula who performed the suburban rites to worship heaven, which had been performed by the ancient Chinese emperors (the vassal states of Silla and Goguryeo did not perform suburban rites out of respect for the emperor) through the Baekje royal family . {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}}
The current Shihohai ritual is said to have begun at the Imperial Court during the reign of [[Emperor Saga]] in the early [[Heian period]] (early [[9th century]] ). It is believed that the ritual was established during the reign of Emperor Uda (late 9th century), and the oldest record of Shihohai being performed is on [[Kanpyō (era)|New Year]] 's Day of the second year of Kanpyo (January 25, [[890]] in [[Julian calendar|the Julian]] calendar), as recorded in the " Uda Tenno Goki ."
Emperor Uda wrote, "Our country is a divine country. Therefore, every morning I pay homage to the large, medium and small deities in the four directions. This begins from now. From now on I will not neglect it even for a single day" (Uda Tenno Goki, entry for October 19, 4th year of the Ninna era). It is believed that the institution of this "daily morning worship" was founded on the premise of the "New Year's Day worship in all four directions" established during the Kōnin era of {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}} .
Disasters such as [[disease]], epidemics, [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], fires, and [[Natural disaster|natural]] disasters were all believed to be caused by the curse of [[Deity|the gods]], and [[Deity|the gods]] who caused the curses were likened to [[Oni (folklore)|demons]] or feared as gods of plague . {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007}} {{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005}} Onmyodo was developed as a form of magic based on the aristocratic society of the Heian period, and many of [[神祇祭祀|the Shinto rituals]] under the Ritsuryo system included yin and yang elements {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} . Various rituals were performed, such as [[疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God]], [[鎮花祭|the Festival for the Chinka Flower]], the Festival [[風神祭|for the Wind God]], the {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|lt=Great Purification|en}}, the Festival for the Plague God [[宮城四隅疫神祭|in the Four Corners of the Palace]], [[防解火災祭|the Firefly]] [[螢惑星祭|Planet Festival]], {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} and the Kyoto area was barrier-bound (secular and sacred areas) and rituals for the "four corners and four boundaries" such as the [[京城四隅疫神祭|Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (capital) and [[宮城四隅疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (imperial palace) were performed to pray for peace and prosperity in the world {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} .
=== Azuchi-Momoyama period === The persecution and oppression of Onmyōji (practitioners of Japanese esoteric cosmology) by Toyotomi Hideyoshi began, driving those who made a living from prayers and divinations to the provinces, and they rapidly lost power. The number of people who called themselves Onmyōji across the country far exceeded the number of official Onmyōji present in the Onmyōryo (Bureau of Yin-Yang) at the time. During the persecutions of the Sengoku period, even the leading Tsuchimikado family, lost many of their inherited Onmyōdō texts and ritual tools to fire. The most important "Great Law" of Onmyōdō, the Taizan Fukun Festival, also lost its altar, and ritual tools had to be borrowed from Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto to conduct a ground-breaking ceremony at the Imperial Palace. This had a significant impact, and the imperial rituals increasingly took on Shinto characteristics. Meanwhile, under the authorization of the shogunate, Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by the Tachikata Shintō, transformed Onmyōdō into what is known as Jinja Shintō. Before the Meiji era, retired Emperors conducting cloistered rule also occasionally performed the ritual of Shihōhai (worship in all four directions).{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}
In other bows made by the Emperor at Imperial Court ceremonies, the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|lt=regent|en}} or the head of the Shinto priest would sometimes bow on his behalf, but since the Shihohai was a bow to the Emperor's guardian star and parents, no bow was made on his behalf. In the "Kasetsu Ryakuki" written by [[白川雅喬|Masataka Shirakawa]] in the Edo period, he denies that Shihohai is a Shinto ritual, saying that it is a ritual to pay homage to guardian stars and ancestral shrines ("non-divine ritual"), so it is possible that Shihohai was a ritual established under [[Taoism]] or Onmyodo and was originally a ritual unrelated to Shinto {{Sfnp|村和明|2013}} .
Following the Emperor's example, [[Nobility|the nobles]] and commoners also performed Shihohai, praying for a good harvest and good health for the year {{NoteTag|『江家次第』には「関白四方拝」「庶臣儀」に関する記述もある{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}}, but over time it came to remain only as an Imperial Court event {{NoteTag|ただし、江戸時代においても[[摂家]]など一部の公家の間でも四方拝が行われていた記録も残されている。例えば[[元文]]3年（[[1738年]]）の元旦に当時の[[関白]][[一条兼香]]が四方拝の行った時に記録が、彼の日記『兼香公記』に残されており、それによれば、天皇の四方拝と異なり三座が設けられず、山陵に代わって[[藤原氏]]や陰陽道に関わる諸神・諸社への拝礼が行われている{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}} .
The festival was temporarily suspended during [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] in the second half of [[15th century|the 15th century]], but was revived in [[Bunmei]] 7 ( [[1475]] ) during the reign of Emperor Go- Tsuchimikado, and was held in the front garden of the Seiryoden Hall of the Kyoto Imperial Palace until the reign of [[Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Komei]] in the second half of [[19th century|the 19th century]] .
=== Before the Meiji Period === It is said that the ceremony started in Emperor Saga's reign, but it was established in Emperor Uda's reign as an official ceremony, the oldest record of Shihohai being held on January 1, Kampyo 2, was in "Uda tenno gyoki" (the diary of the Emperor Uda).<ref name=":0" />
Subsequently, although the ceremony was interrupted with the [[Ōnin War|Onin War]], it started again in 1475, running from the reign of Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado to that of Emperor Komei; the ceremony was held in the front garden of the Palace of Heian (currently Kyoto Imperial Palace), Seiryo-den.<ref name=":0" />
On January 1, torano koku (at about four o'clock in the morning), the Emperor, wearing Korozen no go-ho at Ryoki-den, came to the east garden of Seiryo-den and prayed for his Zokusho (one of the stars of the Big Dipper, which is said to have destiny depending on the year in which the person was born) and spirits in every direction, or the direction of his parents' [https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Imperial%20Mausoleum.html Imperial Mausoleum], whereupon he wished for the peace and security of the nation and good harvests for the coming year.<ref name=":0" />
The chanting words on this ceremony are described in '[https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Dairi%20(the%20Imperial%20palace).html Dairi] [https://www.japanesewiki.com/history/Gishiki%20(Book).html Gishiki]' and 'Go-ke Shidai.'<ref name=":0" />
According to these materials, it is mentioned as Zokuko shichu kado ga shin, Dokuma shichu kado ga shin, Kiyaku shichu kado ga shin, Goki rokugai shichu kado ga shin, Hyakubyo joyu, Shoyoku zuishin, Kyukyu nyoritsu ryo.<ref name=":0" />
=== After the Meiji Period === After the Meiji period, it was regulated by Ordinance No. 1 of Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household), Koshitu Saishi Rei (Imperial Household Religious Rites) (1908). Prior to World War I, it was called Shiho-setsu and was conducted as a national ceremony, being considered one of the biggest of four major ceremonies held on national public holidays.<ref name=":0" />
After the war, the ceremony was continued along with Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household) ordinance, although this law was eventually abolished.<ref name=":0" />
After the war, the ceremony's name was changed to 'Shihohai' and it was conducted as a private function of the Imperial Family.<ref name=":0" />
On January 1, at about 5:30 in the morning, the Emperor, wearing a traditional formal court dress called Korozen no go-ho, would enter a building constructed in the southern garden of Shinka-den, which is located west of the Three Shrines in the Imperial Court, whereupon he would bow toward the direction of two shrines--Ko-tai jingu Shrine and Toyouke Dai-jingu Shrine of Ise-jingu Shrine--and pray to spirits in various directions.<ref name=":0" />
The Imperial mausoleums and Gods the Emperor prays for are, the Ise-jingu Shrine, Tenjin Chigi/all gods, Emperor Jimmu, former three Emperor's mausoleum (Fushimi Momoyama Imperial Mausoleum of Emperor Meiji, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Taisho, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Showa), Ichi no miya Shrine in Musashi Province (Hikawa-jinja Shrine), Ichi no miya Shrine in Yamashiro Province (Kamowake ikazuchi-jinja Shrine and Kamo mioya-jinja Shrine), Iwashimizu Hachimangu Shrine, Atsuta-jingu Shrine, Kashima-jingu Shrine and Katori-jingu Shrine.<ref name=":0" />
== History ==
=== Ceremony before the Meiji period === At the hour of [[Tiger (zodiac)|the tiger]] on January 1st (around 4:00 a.m.), [[Emperor of Japan|the Emperor]] puts on a yellow-dyed robe at [[綾綺殿|the Ayakiden Hall]] of the Imperial Palace and appears in the east garden of Seiryoden . '''Three seats''' have already been set up in the eastern garden of Seiryoden: the Shosei Gohaigoza, the Shiho Gohaigoza, and the Yamaryo Gohaigoza.
The Emperor first sits on the "Zokusei Gohai-za" (a seat for worshipping the Emperor's star) and bows to the Emperor's assigned star {{NoteTag|属星（ぞくしょう）とは、誕生年によって定まるという人間の運命を司る[[北斗七星]]のなかの星のことで、子年は貪狼星（ドゥーベ）、丑年と亥年は巨門星（メラク）、寅年と戌年は禄存星（フェクダ）、卯年と酉年は文曲星（メグレズ）、辰年と申年は廉貞星（アリオト）、巳年と未年は武曲星（ミザール）、午年は破軍星（アルカイド、ベネトナシュ）となる<ref>{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}</ref>。}} . Next, they sit on the "Shiho Gohai-za" (four-direction worship seat) and offer prayers to the divine spirits of the four directions of heaven and earth. Finally, the person sits on the "Yama-Ryo Gohai-Oza" (pilgrimage seat) and bows in the direction of the parents' mountain tombs (omitted if the parents are still alive). Each of them prayed for the safety of the emperor and the extension of his reign. It is also known that during the Edo period, after the worship of the subordinate star, worship was made at the 'Jusei Gohaigoza' to the Naishidokoro and Ise Grand [[Ise Grand Shrine|Shrine]], and before the worship of the tombs of one's parents, worship was added to the mountain tombs of past emperors (the objects of worship varied depending on the period) at the 'Yamaryo Gohaigoza'. Regarding worship at Ise Shrine, there is an entry in the " Diary of Emperor Hanazono " [[Gen'ō|for]] January 1320 which states that this was a custom since the time of {{ill|Go-Fukakusa|lt=Emperor Go-Fukakusa|en}}, and it is believed that what was practiced by the Emperor in the Middle Ages was later adopted as the Emperor's four-way worship.
During this bow, the Emperor recited unique words (spells). According to " The Imperial Court Ceremonies " and " The Eke Ceremonies, " it is as follows.
Some historical sources refer to the "five perils" as the "five misfortunes."
Furthermore, before the Meiji period, the ritual implements used in the New Year's Day four-way worship included the " '''Great Song Folding Screen''' ," but "Great Song" referred to the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern Dynasties in China, and it has been said that the Mingtang ritual, an imperial ritual to worship heaven and earth in the Han dynasty, was inherited by Japan via the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern Dynasties. It has also been said that the yellow-dyed robe worn by the emperor in the New Year's Day four-way worship represents the earth king "yellow," who is at the center of the " monthly law " thought, and that this is related to the imperial rituals of ancient China. {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}}
According to "The Imperial Court Ceremonies" and "The Nishinomiya-ki," on New Year's Day, at the hour of the ox when the rooster crows (2:00 a.m.), four folding screens are set up in the eastern garden, and a lamp is lit in front of the seats for worshiping the divine star, and incense is burned and flowers are placed on plain wooden desks in front of each seat. The ceremony begins at the hour of the tiger (3:00 a.m.). The ritual order is as follows: 1. Worship of the affiliated star. 2. Prostration to the four directions of heaven and earth. 3. (Parents) Two worships. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
=== After the Meiji Period === After the Meiji period, from the viewpoint of {{Ill|Kokugaku|en}}, the influence of [[Taoism]] (belief in the Big Dipper and spells such as the Suiho-Ritsuryo system) was eliminated, and it was reconstructed as a Shinto ritual. It was held as a national event, called '''the Shiho-Setsu festival''', and was considered one of the four major festivals among national holidays.
; Ceremony procedure after the Meiji period : Prior to the ceremony, a temporary structure is set up in the south garden of Shinkaden, an annex to the Imperial Palace and the Three Palace Sanctuaries, with [[簾薦|a bamboo blind]] laid out in the center and two pairs of folding screens arranged around it, a throne set up within it, and two [[灯台 (照明器具)|lighthouses]] provided. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dons a yellow-dyed robe at [[綾綺殿|Ayakiden]] and is led by the Grand Master of Ceremonies out into the south garden of Shinkaden. At the worship throne, after bowing towards both the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Grand Shrines, Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu, they then bow to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor pays respects at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]], the gods of heaven and earth, [[Emperor Jimmu|the tomb of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors, [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya]] of Musashi [[Musashi Province|Province]] ( Hikawa Shrine), [[Yamashiro Province|the Ichinomiya of]] Yamashiro Province ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]] [[Atsuta Shrine|Hachiman Shrine, Atsuta Shrine]], [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya]] of Hitachi Province ( [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima Shrine]] ), and [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya of Shimousa Province]] ( Katori Shrine ), in that order. After completing the four-way worship, the Emperor pays respects at each of the three Imperial shrines (the Kashikodokoro, the Imperial Ancestors' Shrine, and the Shinto Shrine). : The custom of not performing proxy worship in the event that the Emperor has an accident and is unable to perform the four-way worship remains the same as before.
On New Year's Day in 1945, during World War II, air raid sirens sounded to warn of the impending attack of [[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|B-29 bombers]], but [[Hirohito|Emperor Showa]] used the Gobunko library, which was being used as an air raid shelter, as a makeshift funeral hall and performed a four-way worship ceremony. {{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015}}

{{Japanese Imperial Rituals}}'''Shihohai''' [[Ritual|is a ritual]] in which [[Emperor of Japan|the Emperor]] pays homage to the gods of the four directions in the Imperial Palace gardens early in the morning on [[January 1|January 1st]] ( [[New Year's Day]] ) every year. This is an imperial ritual in which people bow in all four directions and pray for the elimination of annual disasters and for a bountiful harvest . {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}}
Shihohai is the name of ceremony held at Imperial Palace in the beginning of the year.
The {{ill|Shihōhai|ja|四方拝}} (Shihōhai) is a ritual performed by the Emperor at dawn on January 1st (New Year's Day), prior to the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}} (New Year's ceremony). It takes place in the south garden of the {{ill|Jingū Kaikan|ja|神嘉殿}} within the Imperial Palace, where the Emperor pays homage to the deities of heaven and earth in all directions. The ceremony is held outdoors, symbolizing the Emperor's descent to the earth to pay respect to the heavenly and earthly deities, referred to as "Tegami-no-Mi" or descending to the garden.
From the early Meiji era, when national holidays were officially designated, until around 1945, January 1st was known as "Shihō no Setsu." Article 23 of the Imperial Household Ceremonial Code (Meiji 41, Imperial Household Ordinance No. 1) stipulated that the Shihōhai should be performed before the Saitan-sai on New Year's Day, except during the Emperor's mourning period or other exceptional circumstances. After this ordinance was abolished in 1947, the ritual continued as a private event in the Imperial family according to former practices.
The gist of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year's Day), the Emperor dons a formal [[Sokutai|robe]] called [[:ja:黄櫨染御袍|']]{{ill|kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}' and enters a temporary building set up in the garden to the south of [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Shinkaden]], which is located to the west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|en}}, and bows toward both the Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu shrines of [[Ise Grand Shrine]], then makes bows to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor worships at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Shrine, the {{Ill|Amatsukami|lt=gods of heaven|en}} and {{Ill|Kunitsukami|lt=earth|en}}, the tomb [[Emperor Jimmu|of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors {{NoteTag|[[上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|上皇]][[明仁]]の場合、曾祖父・[[明治天皇]]の[[伏見桃山陵]]、祖父・[[大正天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|多摩陵]]、父・[[昭和天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|武蔵野陵]]の三陵。}}, the [[Ichinomiya|Ichinomiyas]] of many provinces: [[Musashi Province]] ( {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|lt=Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|en}}), [[Yamashiro Province]] ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine]] , [[Atsuta Shrine]], [[Hitachi Province|the Ichinomiya of Hitachi]] [[Ichinomiya|Province]] ( [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima Shrine]] ), and the Ichinomiya of [[Shimōsa Province|Shimousa Province]] ( {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮}} ). == overview == Shihohai is a ritual in which the Emperor pays respects to the gods of the four directions of heaven and earth in the southern garden of the Shinkaden Hall in the Imperial Palace early in the morning on January 1st (New Year's Day ) every year, prior to the New Year's Festival. The reason why the ceremony is held in the garden rather than on the palace grounds is said to signify that the Emperor himself descends to earth, abdicates and bows down to the gods of heaven and earth, and this is referred to as the " '''Teijo-no-uego''' " ceremony {{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966}} .
From the early Meiji period, when the holiday was legally established, until around [[1945]] (Showa 20), January 1st, the day when this [[:ja:宮中祭祀|Imperial Court ritual]] was held, was called '''Shiho-setsu''' . Article 23 of the [[:ja:皇室祭祀令|Imperial Household Rites Order]] (Imperial Household Order No. 1 of 1908), one of the Imperial Household Ordinances, stipulates that "On the day of the New Year's Ceremony, a ceremony of worship in all four directions shall be held first...However, if the Emperor passes away or there are other circumstances, the ceremony of worship in all four directions shall not be held." After the order was abolished in [[1947]], the New Year's Ceremony has been held in accordance with the old rules as a private event of [[Imperial House of Japan|the Imperial Household]] .
The Shihohai in [[2009]] (Heisei 21) was held at the Imperial Palace due to the simplification of the rituals following the aging of the then Emperor [[Akihito]] (the 125th Emperor).
== Overview == During the early Heian period, this ceremony originated in the Imperial Palace and spread to lords and ordinary people as a wish to be in full harvest and a perfect state of health by praying in various directions no matter what the year might bring, but as time went by the ceremony remained simply as a court function.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Yu|first=A. C.|title=Shihohai - Japanese Wiki Corpus|url=https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Shihohai.html|access-date=2024-04-15|website=www.japanesewiki.com}}</ref>
== The origin of Shihohai == There are different theories that it originated in the Way of Yin and Yang or it came from China, but there are no written materials to show the exact history of how it started.<ref name=":0" />
It is believed to be true that Shihohai is a cultural ceremony that came from China and was changed to suit the Japanese culture while retaining various aspects of Chinese culture, since the Way of Yin and Yan originally came from China and has been systematized, including Chinese studies, thinking, magic and rituals.<ref name=":0" />
== History ==
=== Asuka Period: === The first recorded documented instance of the Shihohai in Japan was in the “Nihon Shoki” ( [[Nihon Shoki|Chronicles of Japan]] ), in the entry for the first day of August in the first year of the reign of [[Empress Kōgyoku]] . {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957}} It is said that at Minami-buchi, the Emperor “bowed in all four directions and looked up to the heavens in prayer,” and this is said to be the very beginning of the custom. {{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957}} The purpose of Empress Kogyoku's worship in all four directions at this time was to pray for [[Rain dance|rain]], but since it was the emperor's personal worship and the act was called "shihohai," it is believed to have been influenced in some way by the shihohai that was institutionalized during the Heian period. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{NoteTag|皇極天皇の漢風諡号の「皇極」と重祚した時の「斉明」は中国古典に由来するが共に「中央」や北斗七星と関連がある語である{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}。}}
In addition, the imperial tombs of the Asuka and [[Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyo]] periods were octagonal tombs, and the Takamikura in the Daigokuden Hall was also octagonal in shape, which suggests that Fujiwara-kyo was the location of rituals demonstrating control over and peace in the entire land in all directions. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} For this reason, it is said that the prohibition of vicariously worshipping may be related to the Emperor's sovereign right to worship the North Star. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
=== Heian Period: === The formalization of Shihōhai during the Heian period is believed to have been influenced by the suburban sacrifices (Jiao sacrifices) of ancient Chinese emperors. Emperor Saga initiated the ceremony in the early Heian period at the Imperial Court. It was standardized during the reign of Emperor Uda with the earliest recorded ceremony conducted in 890 AD, according to the "Uda Tennō ki."
Azuchi-Momoyama Period: During Toyotomi Hideyoshi's rule, Onmyōji faced suppression, which disrupted traditional practices and led to the loss of significant ritual tools and texts, even for leading families such as the Tsuchimikado. The most significant rites of Onmyōdō, like the {{ill|Taizan Fukun Festival|ja|泰山府君祭}}, suffered greatly. Under the shogunate's authority, Onmyōdō was gradually integrated with Shinto practices through figures like Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by Tachikata Shintō, reforming it into {{ill|Shrine Shinto|ja|神社神道}}.
=== Before the Meiji Era: === Retired emperors during the cloistered rule performed Shihōhai, reflecting its importance in both imperial and religious contexts of Japan.
During other imperial ceremonies, regents or officials might perform rituals on behalf of the Emperor, but Shihōhai was always performed personally by the Emperor as it involved paying homage to protective stars and ancestral spirits, aligning with its origins in Daoism and Onmyōdō rather than Shinto.
In time, the practice of Shihōhai spread beyond the Imperial family, with nobles and commoners performing it for a prosperous and healthy year. However, over the centuries, it remained primarily a court ceremony.
=== Meiji Era and Later === Before Meiji: The ceremony on January 1 involved the Emperor wearing a kōrozen no gohō, performing rituals in the Imperial Palace's eastern garden at designated ritual sites. These rituals included paying respects to the Emperor's guardian stars, the deities of all directions, and ancestral tombs.
Post-Meiji: From the Meiji period onward, the influence of Daoism and related esoteric practices was removed, and Shihōhai was reconstructed as a purely Shinto ritual and incorporated into national ceremonies, becoming known as one of the four major seasonal festivals.
== History ==
=== Heian period === The establishment of the Shihohai system during the Heian period is said to have been influenced by the ancient Chinese imperial rituals known as suburban worship, which were performed by [[Emperor Kanmu]] . This was supposedly done with the support of the Baekje king, who was the only person on the Korean peninsula who performed the suburban rites to worship heaven, which had been performed by the ancient Chinese emperors (the vassal states of Silla and Goguryeo did not perform suburban rites out of respect for the emperor) through the Baekje royal family . {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}}
The current Shihohai ritual is said to have begun at the Imperial Court during the reign of [[Emperor Saga]] in the early [[Heian period]] (early [[9th century]] ). It is believed that the ritual was established during the reign of Emperor Uda (late 9th century), and the oldest record of Shihohai being performed is on [[Kanpyō (era)|New Year]] 's Day of the second year of Kanpyo (January 25, [[890]] in [[Julian calendar|the Julian]] calendar), as recorded in the " Uda Tenno Goki ."
Emperor Uda wrote, "Our country is a divine country. Therefore, every morning I pay homage to the large, medium and small deities in the four directions. This begins from now. From now on I will not neglect it even for a single day" (Uda Tenno Goki, entry for October 19, 4th year of the Ninna era). It is believed that the institution of this "daily morning worship" was founded on the premise of the "New Year's Day worship in all four directions" established during the Kōnin era of {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}} .
Disasters such as [[disease]], epidemics, [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], fires, and [[Natural disaster|natural]] disasters were all believed to be caused by the curse of [[Deity|the gods]], and [[Deity|the gods]] who caused the curses were likened to [[Oni (folklore)|demons]] or feared as gods of plague . {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007}} {{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005}} Onmyodo was developed as a form of magic based on the aristocratic society of the Heian period, and many of [[神祇祭祀|the Shinto rituals]] under the Ritsuryo system included yin and yang elements {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} . Various rituals were performed, such as [[疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God]], [[鎮花祭|the Festival for the Chinka Flower]], the Festival [[風神祭|for the Wind God]], the {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|lt=Great Purification|en}}, the Festival for the Plague God [[宮城四隅疫神祭|in the Four Corners of the Palace]], [[防解火災祭|the Firefly]] [[螢惑星祭|Planet Festival]], {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} and the Kyoto area was barrier-bound (secular and sacred areas) and rituals for the "four corners and four boundaries" such as the [[京城四隅疫神祭|Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (capital) and [[宮城四隅疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (imperial palace) were performed to pray for peace and prosperity in the world {{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfnp|林淳|2005}} .
=== Azuchi-Momoyama period === The persecution and oppression of Onmyōji (practitioners of Japanese esoteric cosmology) by Toyotomi Hideyoshi began, driving those who made a living from prayers and divinations to the provinces, and they rapidly lost power. The number of people who called themselves Onmyōji across the country far exceeded the number of official Onmyōji present in the Onmyōryo (Bureau of Yin-Yang) at the time. During the persecutions of the Sengoku period, even the leading Tsuchimikado family, lost many of their inherited Onmyōdō texts and ritual tools to fire. The most important "Great Law" of Onmyōdō, the Taizan Fukun Festival, also lost its altar, and ritual tools had to be borrowed from Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto to conduct a ground-breaking ceremony at the Imperial Palace. This had a significant impact, and the imperial rituals increasingly took on Shinto characteristics. Meanwhile, under the authorization of the shogunate, Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by the Tachikata Shintō, transformed Onmyōdō into what is known as Jinja Shintō. Before the Meiji era, retired Emperors conducting cloistered rule also occasionally performed the ritual of Shihōhai (worship in all four directions).{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}
In other bows made by the Emperor at Imperial Court ceremonies, the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|lt=regent|en}} or the head of the Shinto priest would sometimes bow on his behalf, but since the Shihohai was a bow to the Emperor's guardian star and parents, no bow was made on his behalf. In the "Kasetsu Ryakuki" written by [[白川雅喬|Masataka Shirakawa]] in the Edo period, he denies that Shihohai is a Shinto ritual, saying that it is a ritual to pay homage to guardian stars and ancestral shrines ("non-divine ritual"), so it is possible that Shihohai was a ritual established under [[Taoism]] or Onmyodo and was originally a ritual unrelated to Shinto {{Sfnp|村和明|2013}} .
Following the Emperor's example, [[Nobility|the nobles]] and commoners also performed Shihohai, praying for a good harvest and good health for the year {{NoteTag|『江家次第』には「関白四方拝」「庶臣儀」に関する記述もある{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}}, but over time it came to remain only as an Imperial Court event {{NoteTag|ただし、江戸時代においても[[摂家]]など一部の公家の間でも四方拝が行われていた記録も残されている。例えば[[元文]]3年（[[1738年]]）の元旦に当時の[[関白]][[一条兼香]]が四方拝の行った時に記録が、彼の日記『兼香公記』に残されており、それによれば、天皇の四方拝と異なり三座が設けられず、山陵に代わって[[藤原氏]]や陰陽道に関わる諸神・諸社への拝礼が行われている{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}} .
The festival was temporarily suspended during [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] in the second half of [[15th century|the 15th century]], but was revived in [[Bunmei]] 7 ( [[1475]] ) during the reign of Emperor Go- Tsuchimikado, and was held in the front garden of the Seiryoden Hall of the Kyoto Imperial Palace until the reign of [[Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Komei]] in the second half of [[19th century|the 19th century]] .
=== Before the Meiji Period === It is said that the ceremony started in Emperor Saga's reign, but it was established in Emperor Uda's reign as an official ceremony, the oldest record of Shihohai being held on January 1, Kampyo 2, was in "Uda tenno gyoki" (the diary of the Emperor Uda).<ref name=":0" />
Subsequently, although the ceremony was interrupted with the [[Ōnin War|Onin War]], it started again in 1475, running from the reign of Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado to that of Emperor Komei; the ceremony was held in the front garden of the Palace of Heian (currently Kyoto Imperial Palace), Seiryo-den.<ref name=":0" />
On January 1, torano koku (at about four o'clock in the morning), the Emperor, wearing Korozen no go-ho at Ryoki-den, came to the east garden of Seiryo-den and prayed for his Zokusho (one of the stars of the [[Ursa Major|Big Dipper]], which is said to have destiny depending on the year in which the person was born) and spirits in every direction, or the direction of his parents' {{ill|Japanese imperial tombs|lt=Imperial Mausoleum|fr|Tombes impériales japonaises|en}}, whereupon he wished for the peace and security of the nation and good harvests for the coming year.<ref name=":0" />
The chanting words on this ceremony are described in '{{Ill|Dairi (Japon)|lt=Dairi|fr|Dairi (Japon)|ja|内裏}} [https://www.japanesewiki.com/history/Gishiki%20(Book).html Gishiki]' and 'Go-ke Shidai.'<ref name=":0" />
According to these materials, it is mentioned as Zokuko shichu kado ga shin, Dokuma shichu kado ga shin, Kiyaku shichu kado ga shin, Goki rokugai shichu kado ga shin, Hyakubyo joyu, Shoyoku zuishin, Kyukyu nyoritsu ryo.<ref name=":0" />
=== After the Meiji Period === After the Meiji period, it was regulated by Ordinance No. 1 of Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household), Koshitu Saishi Rei (Imperial Household Religious Rites) (1908). Prior to World War I, it was called Shiho-setsu and was conducted as a national ceremony, being considered one of the biggest of four major ceremonies held on national public holidays.<ref name=":0" />
After the war, the ceremony was continued along with Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household) ordinance, although this law was eventually abolished.<ref name=":0" />
After the war, the ceremony's name was changed to 'Shihohai' and it was conducted as a private function of the Imperial Family.<ref name=":0" />
On January 1, at about 5:30 in the morning, the Emperor, wearing a traditional formal court dress called Korozen no go-ho, would enter a building constructed in the southern garden of Shinka-den, which is located west of the Three Shrines in the Imperial Court, whereupon he would bow toward the direction of two shrines--Ko-tai jingu Shrine and Toyouke Dai-jingu Shrine of Ise-jingu Shrine--and pray to spirits in various directions.<ref name=":0" />
The Imperial mausoleums and Gods the Emperor prays for are, the Ise-jingu Shrine, Tenjin Chigi/all gods, Emperor Jimmu, former three Emperor's mausoleum (Fushimi Momoyama Imperial Mausoleum of Emperor Meiji, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Taisho, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Showa), Ichi no miya Shrine in Musashi Province (Hikawa-jinja Shrine), Ichi no miya Shrine in Yamashiro Province (Kamowake ikazuchi-jinja Shrine and Kamo mioya-jinja Shrine), Iwashimizu Hachimangu Shrine, Atsuta-jingu Shrine, Kashima-jingu Shrine and Katori-jingu Shrine.<ref name=":0" />
== History ==
=== Ceremony before the Meiji period === At the hour of [[Tiger (zodiac)|the tiger]] on January 1st (around 4:00 a.m.), [[Emperor of Japan|the Emperor]] puts on a yellow-dyed robe at [[綾綺殿|the Ayakiden Hall]] of the Imperial Palace and appears in the east garden of Seiryoden . '''Three seats''' have already been set up in the eastern garden of Seiryoden: the Shosei Gohaigoza, the Shiho Gohaigoza, and the Yamaryo Gohaigoza.
The Emperor first sits on the "Zokusei Gohai-za" (a seat for worshipping the Emperor's star) and bows to the Emperor's assigned star {{NoteTag|属星（ぞくしょう）とは、誕生年によって定まるという人間の運命を司る[[北斗七星]]のなかの星のことで、子年は貪狼星（ドゥーベ）、丑年と亥年は巨門星（メラク）、寅年と戌年は禄存星（フェクダ）、卯年と酉年は文曲星（メグレズ）、辰年と申年は廉貞星（アリオト）、巳年と未年は武曲星（ミザール）、午年は破軍星（アルカイド、ベネトナシュ）となる<ref>{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}</ref>。}} . Next, they sit on the "Shiho Gohai-za" (four-direction worship seat) and offer prayers to the divine spirits of the four directions of heaven and earth. Finally, the person sits on the "Yama-Ryo Gohai-Oza" (pilgrimage seat) and bows in the direction of the parents' mountain tombs (omitted if the parents are still alive). Each of them prayed for the safety of the emperor and the extension of his reign. It is also known that during the Edo period, after the worship of the subordinate star, worship was made at the 'Jusei Gohaigoza' to the Naishidokoro and Ise Grand [[Ise Grand Shrine|Shrine]], and before the worship of the tombs of one's parents, worship was added to the mountain tombs of past emperors (the objects of worship varied depending on the period) at the 'Yamaryo Gohaigoza'. Regarding worship at Ise Shrine, there is an entry in the " Diary of Emperor Hanazono " [[Gen'ō|for]] January 1320 which states that this was a custom since the time of {{ill|Go-Fukakusa|lt=Emperor Go-Fukakusa|en}}, and it is believed that what was practiced by the Emperor in the Middle Ages was later adopted as the Emperor's Shihohai.
During this bow, the Emperor recited unique words (spells). According to " The Imperial Court Ceremonies " and " The Eke Ceremonies, " it is as follows.
Some historical sources refer to the "five perils" as the "five misfortunes."
Furthermore, before the Meiji period, the ritual implements used in the New Year's Day Shihohai included the " '''Great Song Folding Screen''' ," but "Great Song" referred to the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern Dynasties in China, and it has been said that the Mingtang ritual, an imperial ritual to worship heaven and earth in the Han dynasty, was inherited by Japan via the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern Dynasties. It has also been said that the yellow-dyed robe worn by the emperor in the New Year's Day Shihohai represents the earth king "yellow," who is at the center of the " monthly law " thought, and that this is related to the imperial rituals of ancient China. {{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011}}
According to "The Imperial Court Ceremonies" and "The Nishinomiya-ki," on New Year's Day, at the hour of the ox when the rooster crows (2:00 a.m.), four folding screens are set up in the eastern garden, and a lamp is lit in front of the seats for worshiping the divine star, and incense is burned and flowers are placed on plain wooden desks in front of each seat. The ceremony begins at the hour of the tiger (3:00 a.m.). The ritual order is as follows: 1. Worship of the affiliated star. 2. Prostration to the four directions of heaven and earth. 3. (Parents) Two worships. {{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
=== After the Meiji Period === After the Meiji period, from the viewpoint of {{Ill|Kokugaku|en}}, the influence of [[Taoism]] (belief in the Big Dipper and spells such as the Suiho-Ritsuryo system) was eliminated, and it was reconstructed as a Shinto ritual. It was held as a national event, called '''the Shiho-Setsu festival''', and was considered one of the four major festivals among national holidays.
; Ceremony procedure after the Meiji period : Prior to the ceremony, a temporary structure is set up in the south garden of Shinkaden, an annex to the Imperial Palace and the Three Palace Sanctuaries, with [[簾薦|a bamboo blind]] laid out in the center and two pairs of folding screens arranged around it, a throne set up within it, and two [[灯台 (照明器具)|lighthouses]] provided. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dons a yellow-dyed robe at [[綾綺殿|Ayakiden]] and is led by the Grand Master of Ceremonies out into the south garden of Shinkaden. At the worship throne, after bowing towards both the [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Grand Shrines, Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu, they then bow to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor pays respects at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]], the gods of heaven and earth, [[Emperor Jimmu|the tomb of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors, [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya]] of Musashi [[Musashi Province|Province]] ( Hikawa Shrine), [[Yamashiro Province|the Ichinomiya of]] Yamashiro Province ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]] [[Atsuta Shrine|Hachiman Shrine, Atsuta Shrine]], [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya]] of Hitachi Province ( [[Kashima-jingū|Kashima Shrine]] ), and [[Ichinomiya|the Ichinomiya of Shimousa Province]] ( Katori Shrine ), in that order. After completing the Shihohai, the Emperor pays respects at each of the three Imperial shrines (the Kashikodokoro, the Imperial Ancestors' Shrine, and the Shinto Shrine). : The custom of not performing proxy worship in the event that the Emperor has an accident and is unable to perform the Shihohai remains the same as before.
On New Year's Day in 1945, during World War II, air raid sirens sounded to warn of the impending attack of [[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|B-29 bombers]], but [[Hirohito|Emperor Showa]] used the Gobunko library, which was being used as an air raid shelter, as a makeshift funeral hall and performed a Shihohai ceremony. {{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015}}
