'''Shihohai''' is a ritual in which the [[Emperor of Japan]] pays homage to the gods of the four directions in the {{ill|Imperial Palace East Garden|en}} early in the morning on [[January 1|January 1st]] ( [[New Year's Day]] ) every year. This is an imperial ritual in which people bow in all four directions and pray for the elimination of annual disasters and for a bountiful harvest . {{Sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfn|林淳|2005}} [[en:draft:Shihohai]] Shihohai is the name of ceremony held at Imperial Palace in the beginning of the year.
The {{ill|Shihōhai|ja|四方拝}} (Shihōhai) is a ritual performed by the Emperor at dawn on January 1st (New Year's Day), prior to the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}} (New Year's ceremony). It takes place in the south garden of the {{ill|Jingū Kaikan|ja|神嘉殿}} within the Imperial Palace, where the Emperor pays homage to the deities of heaven and earth in all directions. The ceremony is held outdoors, symbolizing the Emperor's descent to the earth to pay respect to the heavenly and earthly deities, referred to as "Tegami-no-Mi" or descending to the garden.
From the early Meiji era, when national holidays were officially designated, until around 1945, January 1st was known as "Shihō no Setsu." Article 23 of the Imperial Household Ceremonial Code (Meiji 41, Imperial Household Ordinance No. 1) stipulated that the Shihōhai should be performed before the Saitan-sai on New Year's Day, except during the Emperor's mourning period or other exceptional circumstances. After this ordinance was abolished in 1947, the ritual continued as a private event in the Imperial family according to former practices. == Overview == Shihohai is a ritual in which the Emperor pays respects to the gods of the four directions of heaven and earth in the southern garden of the Shinkaden Hall in the Imperial Palace early in the morning on January 1st (New Year's Day ) every year, prior to the New Year's Festival. The reason why the ceremony is held in the garden rather than on the palace grounds is said to signify that the Emperor himself descends to earth, abdicates and bows down to the gods of heaven and earth, and this is referred to as the " '''Teijo-no-uego''' " ceremony {{sfn|松山能夫|1966}} .
During the early Heian period, this ceremony originated in the Imperial Palace and spread to lords and ordinary people as a wish to be in full harvest and a perfect state of health by praying in various directions no matter what the year might bring, but as time went by the ceremony remained simply as a court function.<ref name="Yu">{{Cite web|last=Yu|first=A. C.|title=Shihohai - Japanese Wiki Corpus|url=https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Shihohai.html|access-date=2024-04-15|website=www.japanesewiki.com}}</ref>
From the early Meiji period, when the holiday was legally established, until around [[1945]] (Showa 20), January 1st, the day when this [[:ja:宮中祭祀|Imperial Court ritual]] was held, was called '''Shiho-setsu''' . Article 23 of the [[:ja:皇室祭祀令|Imperial Household Rites Order]] (Imperial Household Order No. 1 of 1908), one of the Imperial Household Ordinances, stipulates that "On the day of the New Year's Ceremony, a ceremony of worship in all four directions shall be held first...However, if the Emperor passes away or there are other circumstances, the ceremony of worship in all four directions shall not be held." After the order was abolished in [[1947]], the New Year's Ceremony has been held in accordance with the old rules as a private event of [[Imperial House of Japan|the Imperial Household]] .
The Shihohai in [[2009]] (Heisei 21) was held at the Imperial Palace due to the simplification of the rituals following the aging of the then Emperor [[Akihito]] (the 125th Emperor).
== Practices == The gist of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year's Day), the Emperor dons a formal [[Sokutai|robe]] called [[:ja:黄櫨染御袍|']]{{ill|kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}' and enters a temporary building set up in the garden to the south of [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Shinkaden]], which is located to the west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|en}}, and bows toward both the Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu shrines of [[Ise Grand Shrine]], then makes bows to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor worships at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Shrine, the {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Amatsukami|lt=gods of heaven|en}} and {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kunitsukami|lt=earth|en}}, the tomb [[Emperor Jimmu|of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors {{NoteTag|[[上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|上皇]][[明仁]]の場合、曾祖父・[[明治天皇]]の[[伏見桃山陵]]、祖父・[[大正天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|多摩陵]]、父・[[昭和天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|武蔵野陵]]の三陵。}}, the [[Ichinomiya|Ichinomiyas]] of many provinces: [[Musashi Province]] ( {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|lt=Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|en}}), [[Yamashiro Province]] ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine]] , [[Atsuta Shrine]], [[Hitachi Province|the Ichinomiya of Hitachi]] [[Ichinomiya|Province]] ( [[Kashima Jingu|Kashima Shrine]] ), and the Ichinomiya of [[Shimōsa Province|Shimousa Province]] ( {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮}} ).
== The origin of Shihohai == There are different theories that it originated in the Way of Yin and Yang or it came from China, but there are no written materials to show the exact history of how it started.<ref name="Yu" />
It is believed to be true that Shihohai is a cultural ceremony that came from China and was changed to suit the Japanese culture while retaining various aspects of Chinese culture, since the Way of Yin and Yan originally came from China and has been systematized, including Chinese studies, thinking, magic and rituals.<ref name="Yu" />
== Asuka Period: == The first recorded documented instance of the Shihohai in Japan was in the “Nihon Shoki” ( [[Nihon Shoki|Chronicles of Japan]] ), in the entry for the first day of August in the first year of the reign of [[Empress Kōgyoku]] . {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{sfn|八束清貫|1957}} It is said that at Minami-buchi, the Emperor “bowed in all four directions and looked up to the heavens in prayer,” and this is said to be the very beginning of the custom. {{sfn|八束清貫|1957}} The purpose of Empress Kogyoku's worship in all four directions at this time was to pray for [[:en:Rain_dance|rain]], but since it was the emperor's personal worship and the act was called "shihohai," it is believed to have been influenced in some way by the shihohai that was institutionalized during the Heian period. {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{NoteTag|皇極天皇の漢風諡号の「皇極」と重祚した時の「斉明」は中国古典に由来するが共に「中央」や北斗七星と関連がある語である{{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}。}}
In addition, the imperial tombs of the Asuka and [[Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyo]] periods were octagonal tombs, and the Takamikura in the Daigokuden Hall was also octagonal in shape, which suggests that Fujiwara-kyo was the location of rituals demonstrating control over and peace in the entire land in all directions. {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} For this reason, it is said that the prohibition of vicariously worshipping may be related to the Emperor's sovereign right to worship the North Star. {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
== Suburban worship in the Heian period == The establishment of the Shihohai system during the Heian period is said to have been influenced by the ancient Chinese imperial rituals known as {{ill|suburban worship|ja|郊祀}}, which were performed by [[Emperor Kanmu]] . This was supposedly done with the support of the Baekje king, who was the only person on the Korean peninsula who performed the suburban rites to worship heaven, which had been performed by the ancient [[List of emperors of China|Chinese emperors]] (the vassal states of Silla and Goguryeo did not perform suburban rites out of respect for the emperor) through the {{ill|Kudara no Konikishi clan|lt=Baekje royal family|en}} . {{sfn|石野浩司|2011}}
Such rituals are called "suburban" since they were performed in the suburbs of the capital, rather than in central areas.
In Japan, the " [[Nihon Shoki]] " (Chronicles of Japan) states [[Emperor Jimmu|that Emperor Jimmu]] established a sacred ground at [[:ja:鳥見山|Mount Torimi]] and performed suburban rituals after ascending to the throne (Jinmu 4th year, February 16, Koshin article), but this is an embellishment made by later generations, and the description of the festival also differs from that of the Chinese suburban rituals.
The first suburban rituals influenced by China were held in Kashiwara (Katano Kashiwara) in Katano County, [[Nagaoka-kyō|Kawachi]] Province, on the southern outskirts of Nagaoka-kyo, on November 10, 4th year of [[Emperor Kanmu|Enryaku]] and November 5, 6th year of [[Katanogahara|Enryaku, as part of Emperor Kanmu]] 's policy of adopting Chinese influence. A small circular hill that existed until the early Showa period in what is now Katahoko, [[Hirakata|Hirakata City,]] [[Osaka Prefecture|Osaka]] Prefecture, is said to be the remains of this shrine. <ref>[[林陸朗]]「交野の郊祀円丘」（『平安時代史事典』角川書店、1994th year 、ISBN 978-4-04-031700-7）P496</ref> On the latter occasion, the emperor's real father, [[Emperor Kōnin|Emperor Kōnin,]] was also enshrined, and [[Ritual text (Chinese)|the ritual text]] adopted the style of Chinese suburban worship, stating, "To the Emperor Haotian" <ref group="注釈">This is the earliest time {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Saimon|ja|祭文}} appears in Japanese literature。[[郊祀#村山|村山（1979）p.43]]</ref> . This was intended to re-establish the [[Ritsuryo system]] through the introduction of Chinese culture, and it is said that the Emperor was familiar with Chinese culture through [[Kazushi|the Wa]] clan, which was descended from immigrants on his mother's side, and that the imperial line of [[Emperor Tenmu|Emperor]] Tenmu had been broken since [[Jinshin Rebellion|the Jinshin War]] and the imperial line of Emperor [[Emperor Tenji|Tenchi]] had been restored, and that the Emperor intended to report this fact to [[Tian|the Emperor]] in Nagaoka-kyo, the capital of the new dynasty.
Afterwards, a suburban ritual was also held in Kashiwara from November 22nd to the following day in the third year of the reign of [[Emperor Montoku]] ( {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|lt=Montoku Jitsuroku|en}} ). However, by this time the capital had already been moved to Heian-kyo long ago, and although Kashiwara was in the southern suburbs of Heian-kyo, it was still far away, leaving many mysteries such as why a new altar was not built in a location closer to Heian-kyo, and why a suburban ritual that had not been recorded and had been carried out for over 70 years since the 6th year of the Enryaku era was revived. Moreover, in Japanese history, it can be confirmed that suburban worship was performed only three times: twice during the Enryaku period and once during the Saikō period, and it is believed that these were the only three times that it was actually performed. Many mysteries remain surrounding the history of suburban rituals in Japan.
== Heian period == The current Shihohai ritual is said to have begun at the Imperial Court during the reign of [[Emperor Saga]] in the early [[Heian period]] (early [[9th century]] ). It is believed that the ritual was established during the reign of Emperor Uda (late 9th century), and the oldest record of Shihohai being performed is on [[Kanpyō (era)|New Year]] 's Day of the second year of Kanpyo (January 25, [[890]] in [[Julian calendar|the Julian]] calendar), as recorded in the " Uda Tenno Goki ."
Emperor Uda wrote, "Our country is a divine country. Therefore, every morning I pay homage to the large, medium and small deities in the four directions. This begins from now. From now on I will not neglect it even for a single day" (Uda Tenno Goki, entry for October 19, 4th year of the Ninna era). It is believed that the institution of this "daily morning worship" was founded on the premise of the "New Year's Day worship in all four directions" established during the Kōnin era of {{sfn|石野浩司|2011}} .
Disasters such as [[disease]], epidemics, [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], fires, and [[Natural disaster|natural]] disasters were all believed to be caused by the curse of [[Deity|the gods]], and [[Deity|the gods]] who caused the curses were likened to [[Oni (folklore)|demons]] or feared as gods of plague . {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|斎藤英喜|2007}} {{sfn|繁田信一|2005}} Onmyodo was developed as a form of magic based on the aristocratic society of the Heian period, and many of [[:ja:神祇祭祀|the Shinto rituals]] under the Ritsuryo system included yin and yang elements {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|林淳|2005}} . Various rituals were performed, such as [[:ja:疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God]], [[:ja:鎮花祭|the Festival for the Chinka Flower]], the Festival [[:ja:風神祭|for the Wind God]], the {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|lt=Great Purification|en}}, the Festival for the Plague God [[:ja:宮城四隅疫神祭|in the Four Corners of the Palace]], [[:ja:防解火災祭|the Firefly]] [[:ja:螢惑星祭|Planet Festival]], {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|林淳|2005}} and the Kyoto area was barrier-bound (secular and sacred areas) and rituals for the "four corners and four boundaries" such as the [[:ja:京城四隅疫神祭|Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (capital) and [[:ja:宮城四隅疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (imperial palace) were performed to pray for peace and prosperity in the world {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|林淳|2005}} .
== Azuchi-Momoyama period == The persecution and oppression of Onmyōji (practitioners of Japanese esoteric cosmology) by [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] began, driving those who made a living from prayers and divinations to the provinces, and they rapidly lost power. The number of people who called themselves Onmyōji across the country far exceeded the number of official Onmyōji present in the Onmyōryo (Bureau of Yin-Yang) at the time. During the persecutions of the Sengoku period, even the leading Tsuchimikado family, lost many of their inherited Onmyōdō texts and ritual tools to fire. The most important "Great Law" of Onmyōdō, the Taizan Fukun Festival, also lost its altar, and ritual tools had to be borrowed from Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto to conduct a ground-breaking ceremony at the Imperial Palace. This had a significant impact, and the imperial rituals increasingly took on Shinto characteristics. Meanwhile, under the authorization of the shogunate, Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by the Tachikata Shintō, transformed Onmyōdō into what is known as Jinja Shintō. Before the Meiji era, retired Emperors conducting cloistered rule also occasionally performed the ritual of Shihōhai (worship in all four directions).{{sfn|小池康寿|2015|p=33}} {{sfn|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}} {{sfn|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}} {{sfn|小池康寿|2015|p=34}} {{sfn|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}} {{sfn|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}} {{sfn|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}} {{sfn|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}
In other bows made by the Emperor at Imperial Court ceremonies, the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|lt=regent|en}} or the head of the Shinto priest would sometimes bow on his behalf, but since the Shihohai was a bow to the Emperor's guardian star and parents, no bow was made on his behalf. In the "Kasetsu Ryakuki" written by [[:ja:白川雅喬|Masataka Shirakawa]] in the Edo period, he denies that Shihohai is a Shinto ritual, saying that it is a ritual to pay homage to guardian stars and ancestral shrines ("non-divine ritual"), so it is possible that Shihohai was a ritual established under [[Taoism]] or Onmyodo and was originally a ritual unrelated to Shinto {{sfn|村和明|2013}} .
Following the Emperor's example, [[Nobility|the nobles]] and commoners also performed Shihohai, praying for a good harvest and good health for the year {{NoteTag|『江家次第』には「関白四方拝」「庶臣儀」に関する記述もある{{要出典|date=2023rd year 12月}}。}}, but over time it came to remain only as an Imperial Court event {{NoteTag|ただし、江戸時代においても[[摂家]]など一部の公家の間でも四方拝が行われていた記録も残されている。例えば[[元文]]3rd year （[[1738]]）の元旦に当時の{{ill|Kanpaku|ja|関白|fr|Kanpaku|ru|Кампаку|sv|Kampaku|uk|Кампаку|zh|關白}}[[一条兼香]]が四方拝の行った時に記録が、彼の日記『兼香公記』に残されており、それによれば、天皇の四方拝と異なり三座が設けられず、山陵に代わって[[藤原氏]]や陰陽道に関わる諸神・諸社への拝礼が行われている{{要出典|date=2023rd year 12月}}。}} .
The festival was temporarily suspended during [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] in the second half of [[15th century|the 15th century]], but was revived in [[Bunmei]] 7 ( [[1475]] ) during the reign of Emperor Go- Tsuchimikado, and was held in the front garden of the Seiryoden Hall of the Kyoto Imperial Palace until the reign of [[Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Komei]] in the second half of [[19th century|the 19th century]] .
== Edo Period == Subsequently, although the ceremony was interrupted with the [[Ōnin War|Onin War]], it started again in 1475, running from the reign of Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado to that of Emperor Komei; the ceremony was held in the front garden of the Palace of Heian (currently Kyoto Imperial Palace), Seiryo-den.<ref name="Yu" />
On January 1, torano koku (at about four o'clock in the morning), the Emperor, wearing Korozen no go-ho at Ryoki-den, came to the east garden of Seiryo-den and prayed for his Zokusho (one of the stars of the [[:en:Ursa_Major|Big Dipper]], which is said to have destiny depending on the year in which the person was born) and spirits in every direction, or the direction of his parents' {{ill|Japanese imperial tombs|lt=Imperial Mausoleum|fr|Tombes impériales japonaises|en}}, whereupon he wished for the peace and security of the nation and good harvests for the coming year.<ref name="Yu" />
The chanting words on this ceremony are described in '{{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Dairi (Japon)|lt=Dairi|fr|Dairi (Japon)|ja|内裏}} [https://www.japanesewiki.com/history/Gishiki%20(Book).html Gishiki]' and 'Go-ke Shidai.'<ref name="Yu" />
According to these materials, it is mentioned as Zokuko shichu kado ga shin, Dokuma shichu kado ga shin, Kiyaku shichu kado ga shin, Goki rokugai shichu kado ga shin, Hyakubyo joyu, Shoyoku zuishin, Kyukyu nyoritsu ryo.<ref name="Yu" />
== After the Meiji Period == After the Meiji period, from the viewpoint of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kokugaku|en}}, the influence of [[Taoism]] (belief in the Big Dipper and spells such as the Suiho-Ritsuryo system) was eliminated, and it was reconstructed as a Shinto ritual. It was held as a national event, called '''the Shiho-Setsu festival''', and was considered one of the four major festivals among national holidays.
After the Meiji period, it was regulated by Ordinance No. 1 of Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household), Koshitu Saishi Rei (Imperial Household Religious Rites) (1908). Prior to World War I, it was called Shiho-setsu and was conducted as a national ceremony, being considered one of the biggest of four major ceremonies held on national public holidays.<ref name="Yu" />
After the war, the ceremony was continued along with Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household) ordinance, although this law was eventually abolished.<ref name="Yu" />
After the war, the ceremony's name was changed to 'Shihohai' and it was conducted as a private function of the Imperial Family.<ref name="Yu" />
On January 1, at about 5:30 in the morning, the Emperor, wearing a traditional formal court dress called Korozen no go-ho, would enter a building constructed in the southern garden of Shinka-den, which is located west of the Three Shrines in the Imperial Court, whereupon he would bow toward the direction of two shrines--Ko-tai jingu Shrine and Toyouke Dai-jingu Shrine of Ise-jingu Shrine--and pray to spirits in various directions.<ref name="Yu" />
The Imperial mausoleums and Gods the Emperor prays for are, the Ise-jingu Shrine, Tenjin Chigi/all gods, Emperor Jimmu, former three Emperor's mausoleum (Fushimi Momoyama Imperial Mausoleum of Emperor Meiji, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Taisho, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Showa), Ichi no miya Shrine in Musashi Province (Hikawa-jinja Shrine), Ichi no miya Shrine in Yamashiro Province (Kamowake ikazuchi-jinja Shrine and Kamo mioya-jinja Shrine), Iwashimizu Hachimangu Shrine, Atsuta-jingu Shrine, Kashima-jingu Shrine and Katori-jingu Shrine.<ref name="Yu" />
On New Year's Day in 1945, during World War II, air raid sirens sounded to warn of the impending attack of [[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|B-29 bombers]], but [[Hirohito|Emperor Showa]] used the Gobunko library, which was being used as an air raid shelter, as a makeshift funeral hall and performed a Shihohai ceremony. {{sfn|藤田尚徳|2015}}

{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}}
{{User:Immanuelle/Japanese Imperial Rituals updated}} {{complex}}
'''Shihohai''' is a ritual in which the [[Emperor of Japan]] pays homage to the gods of the four directions in the {{ill|Imperial Palace East Garden|en}} early in the morning on [[January 1|January 1st]] ( [[New Year's Day]] ) every year. This is an imperial ritual in which people bow in all four directions and pray for the elimination of annual disasters and for a bountiful harvest . {{Sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{Sfn|林淳|2005}} [[en:draft:Shihohai]] Shihohai is the name of ceremony held at Imperial Palace in the beginning of the year.
The {{ill|Shihōhai|ja|四方拝}} (Shihōhai) is a ritual performed by the Emperor at dawn on January 1st (New Year's Day), prior to the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}} (New Year's ceremony). It takes place in the south garden of the {{ill|Jingū Kaikan|ja|神嘉殿}} within the Imperial Palace, where the Emperor pays homage to the deities of heaven and earth in all directions. The ceremony is held outdoors, symbolizing the Emperor's descent to the earth to pay respect to the heavenly and earthly deities, referred to as "Tegami-no-Mi" or descending to the garden.
From the early Meiji era, when national holidays were officially designated, until around 1945, January 1st was known as "Shihō no Setsu." Article 23 of the Imperial Household Ceremonial Code (Meiji 41, Imperial Household Ordinance No. 1) stipulated that the Shihōhai should be performed before the Saitan-sai on New Year's Day, except during the Emperor's mourning period or other exceptional circumstances. After this ordinance was abolished in 1947, the ritual continued as a private event in the Imperial family according to former practices. == Overview == Shihohai is a ritual in which the Emperor pays respects to the gods of the four directions of heaven and earth in the southern garden of the Shinkaden Hall in the Imperial Palace early in the morning on January 1st (New Year's Day ) every year, prior to the New Year's Festival. The reason why the ceremony is held in the garden rather than on the palace grounds is said to signify that the Emperor himself descends to earth, abdicates and bows down to the gods of heaven and earth, and this is referred to as the " '''Teijo-no-uego''' " ceremony {{sfn|松山能夫|1966}} .
During the early Heian period, this ceremony originated in the Imperial Palace and spread to lords and ordinary people as a wish to be in full harvest and a perfect state of health by praying in various directions no matter what the year might bring, but as time went by the ceremony remained simply as a court function.<ref name="Yu">{{Cite web|last=Yu|first=A. C.|title=Shihohai - Japanese Wiki Corpus|url=https://www.japanesewiki.com/emperor/Shihohai.html|access-date=2024-04-15|website=www.japanesewiki.com}}</ref>
From the early Meiji period, when the holiday was legally established, until around [[1945]] (Showa 20), January 1st, the day when this [[:ja:宮中祭祀|Imperial Court ritual]] was held, was called '''Shiho-setsu''' . Article 23 of the [[:ja:皇室祭祀令|Imperial Household Rites Order]] (Imperial Household Order No. 1 of 1908), one of the Imperial Household Ordinances, stipulates that "On the day of the New Year's Ceremony, a ceremony of worship in all four directions shall be held first...However, if the Emperor passes away or there are other circumstances, the ceremony of worship in all four directions shall not be held." After the order was abolished in [[1947]], the New Year's Ceremony has been held in accordance with the old rules as a private event of [[Imperial House of Japan|the Imperial Household]] .
The Shihohai in [[2009]] (Heisei 21) was held at the Imperial Palace due to the simplification of the rituals following the aging of the then Emperor [[Akihito]] (the 125th Emperor).
== Practices == The gist of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year's Day), the Emperor dons a formal [[Sokutai|robe]] called [[:ja:黄櫨染御袍|']]{{ill|kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}' and enters a temporary building set up in the garden to the south of [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Shinkaden]], which is located to the west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|en}}, and bows toward both the Kotai Jingu and Toyouke Daijingu shrines of [[Ise Grand Shrine]], then makes bows to the deities in all four directions. The gods and imperial tombs that the Emperor worships at this time are [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise]] Shrine, the {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Amatsukami|lt=gods of heaven|en}} and {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kunitsukami|lt=earth|en}}, the tomb [[Emperor Jimmu|of Emperor Jimmu]] and the mountain tombs of the three previous emperors {{NoteTag|[[上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|上皇]][[明仁]]の場合、曾祖父・[[明治天皇]]の[[伏見桃山陵]]、祖父・[[大正天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|多摩陵]]、父・[[昭和天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|武蔵野陵]]の三陵。}}, the [[Ichinomiya|Ichinomiyas]] of many provinces: [[Musashi Province]] ( {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|lt=Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|en}}), [[Yamashiro Province]] ( [[Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[Shimogamo Shrine|Kamomioya Shrine]] ), [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine]] , [[Atsuta Shrine]], [[Hitachi Province|the Ichinomiya of Hitachi]] [[Ichinomiya|Province]] ( [[Kashima Jingu|Kashima Shrine]] ), and the Ichinomiya of [[Shimōsa Province|Shimousa Province]] ( {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮}} ).
== The origin of Shihohai == There are different theories that it originated in the Way of Yin and Yang or it came from China, but there are no written materials to show the exact history of how it started.<ref name="Yu" />
It is believed to be true that Shihohai is a cultural ceremony that came from China and was changed to suit the Japanese culture while retaining various aspects of Chinese culture, since the Way of Yin and Yan originally came from China and has been systematized, including Chinese studies, thinking, magic and rituals.<ref name="Yu" />
== Asuka Period: == The first recorded documented instance of the Shihohai in Japan was in the “Nihon Shoki” ( [[Nihon Shoki|Chronicles of Japan]] ), in the entry for the first day of August in the first year of the reign of [[Empress Kōgyoku]] . {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{sfn|八束清貫|1957}} It is said that at Minami-buchi, the Emperor “bowed in all four directions and looked up to the heavens in prayer,” and this is said to be the very beginning of the custom. {{sfn|八束清貫|1957}} The purpose of Empress Kogyoku's worship in all four directions at this time was to pray for [[:en:Rain_dance|rain]], but since it was the emperor's personal worship and the act was called "shihohai," it is believed to have been influenced in some way by the shihohai that was institutionalized during the Heian period. {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} {{NoteTag|皇極天皇の漢風諡号の「皇極」と重祚した時の「斉明」は中国古典に由来するが共に「中央」や北斗七星と関連がある語である{{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}。}}
In addition, the imperial tombs of the Asuka and [[Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyo]] periods were octagonal tombs, and the Takamikura in the Daigokuden Hall was also octagonal in shape, which suggests that Fujiwara-kyo was the location of rituals demonstrating control over and peace in the entire land in all directions. {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}} For this reason, it is said that the prohibition of vicariously worshipping may be related to the Emperor's sovereign right to worship the North Star. {{sfn|渡辺瑞穂子|2020}}
== Suburban worship in the Heian period == The establishment of the Shihohai system during the Heian period is said to have been influenced by the ancient Chinese imperial rituals known as {{ill|suburban worship|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|lt=Jiao sacrifices (suburban worship)}}, which were performed by [[Emperor Kanmu]] . This was supposedly done with the support of the Baekje king, who was the only person on the Korean peninsula who performed the suburban rites to worship heaven, which had been performed by the ancient [[List of emperors of China|Chinese emperors]] (the vassal states of Silla and Goguryeo did not perform suburban rites out of respect for the emperor) through the {{ill|Kudara no Konikishi clan|lt=Baekje royal family|en}} . {{sfn|石野浩司|2011}}
Such rituals are called "suburban" since they were performed in the suburbs of the capital, rather than in central areas.
In Japan, the " [[Nihon Shoki]] " (Chronicles of Japan) states [[Emperor Jimmu|that Emperor Jimmu]] established a sacred ground at [[:ja:鳥見山|Mount Torimi]] and performed suburban rituals after ascending to the throne (Jinmu 4th year, February 16, Koshin article), but this is an embellishment made by later generations, and the description of the festival also differs from that of the Chinese suburban rituals.
The first suburban rituals influenced by China were held in Kashiwara (Katano Kashiwara) in Katano County, [[Nagaoka-kyō|Kawachi]] Province, on the southern outskirts of Nagaoka-kyo, on November 10, 4th year of [[Emperor Kanmu|Enryaku]] and November 5, 6th year of [[Katanogahara|Enryaku, as part of Emperor Kanmu]] 's policy of adopting Chinese influence. A small circular hill that existed until the early Showa period in what is now Katahoko, [[Hirakata|Hirakata City,]] [[Osaka Prefecture|Osaka]] Prefecture, is said to be the remains of this shrine. <ref>[[林陸朗]]「交野の郊祀円丘」（『平安時代史事典』角川書店、1994th year 、ISBN 978-4-04-031700-7）P496</ref> On the latter occasion, the emperor's real father, [[Emperor Kōnin|Emperor Kōnin,]] was also enshrined, and [[Ritual text (Chinese)|the ritual text]] adopted the style of Chinese suburban worship, stating, "To the Emperor Haotian" <ref group="注釈">This is the earliest time {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Saimon|ja|祭文}} appears in Japanese literature。[[郊祀#村山|村山（1979）p.43]]</ref> . This was intended to re-establish the [[Ritsuryo system]] through the introduction of Chinese culture, and it is said that the Emperor was familiar with Chinese culture through [[Kazushi|the Wa]] clan, which was descended from immigrants on his mother's side, and that the imperial line of [[Emperor Tenmu|Emperor]] Tenmu had been broken since [[Jinshin Rebellion|the Jinshin War]] and the imperial line of Emperor [[Emperor Tenji|Tenchi]] had been restored, and that the Emperor intended to report this fact to [[Tian|the Emperor]] in Nagaoka-kyo, the capital of the new dynasty.
Afterwards, a suburban ritual was also held in Kashiwara from November 22nd to the following day in the third year of the reign of [[Emperor Montoku]] ( {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|lt=Montoku Jitsuroku|en}} ). However, by this time the capital had already been moved to Heian-kyo long ago, and although Kashiwara was in the southern suburbs of Heian-kyo, it was still far away, leaving many mysteries such as why a new altar was not built in a location closer to Heian-kyo, and why a suburban ritual that had not been recorded and had been carried out for over 70 years since the 6th year of the Enryaku era was revived. Moreover, in Japanese history, it can be confirmed that suburban worship was performed only three times: twice during the Enryaku period and once during the Saikō period, and it is believed that these were the only three times that it was actually performed. Many mysteries remain surrounding the history of suburban rituals in Japan.
== Heian period == The current Shihohai ritual is said to have begun at the Imperial Court during the reign of [[Emperor Saga]] in the early [[Heian period]] (early [[9th century]] ). It is believed that the ritual was established during the reign of Emperor Uda (late 9th century), and the oldest record of Shihohai being performed is on [[Kanpyō (era)|New Year]] 's Day of the second year of Kanpyo (January 25, [[890]] in [[Julian calendar|the Julian]] calendar), as recorded in the " Uda Tenno Goki ."
Emperor Uda wrote, "Our country is a divine country. Therefore, every morning I pay homage to the large, medium and small deities in the four directions. This begins from now. From now on I will not neglect it even for a single day" (Uda Tenno Goki, entry for October 19, 4th year of the Ninna era). It is believed that the institution of this "daily morning worship" was founded on the premise of the "New Year's Day worship in all four directions" established during the Kōnin era of {{sfn|石野浩司|2011}} .
Disasters such as [[disease]], epidemics, [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], fires, and [[Natural disaster|natural]] disasters were all believed to be caused by the curse of [[Deity|the gods]], and [[Deity|the gods]] who caused the curses were likened to [[Oni (folklore)|demons]] or feared as gods of plague . {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|斎藤英喜|2007}} {{sfn|繁田信一|2005}} Onmyodo was developed as a form of magic based on the aristocratic society of the Heian period, and many of [[:ja:神祇祭祀|the Shinto rituals]] under the Ritsuryo system included yin and yang elements {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|林淳|2005}} . Various rituals were performed, such as [[:ja:疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God]], [[:ja:鎮花祭|the Festival for the Chinka Flower]], the Festival [[:ja:風神祭|for the Wind God]], the {{ill|Ōharae-shiki|lt=Great Purification|en}}, the Festival for the Plague God [[:ja:宮城四隅疫神祭|in the Four Corners of the Palace]], [[:ja:防解火災祭|the Firefly]] [[:ja:螢惑星祭|Planet Festival]], {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|林淳|2005}} and the Kyoto area was barrier-bound (secular and sacred areas) and rituals for the "four corners and four boundaries" such as the [[:ja:京城四隅疫神祭|Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (capital) and [[:ja:宮城四隅疫神祭|the Festival for the Plague God in the Four Corners of the Palace]] (imperial palace) were performed to pray for peace and prosperity in the world {{sfn|小池康寿|2015}} {{sfn|林淳|2005}} .
== Azuchi-Momoyama period == The persecution and oppression of Onmyōji (practitioners of Japanese esoteric cosmology) by [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] began, driving those who made a living from prayers and divinations to the provinces, and they rapidly lost power. The number of people who called themselves Onmyōji across the country far exceeded the number of official Onmyōji present in the Onmyōryo (Bureau of Yin-Yang) at the time. During the persecutions of the Sengoku period, even the leading Tsuchimikado family, lost many of their inherited Onmyōdō texts and ritual tools to fire. The most important "Great Law" of Onmyōdō, the Taizan Fukun Festival, also lost its altar, and ritual tools had to be borrowed from Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto to conduct a ground-breaking ceremony at the Imperial Palace. This had a significant impact, and the imperial rituals increasingly took on Shinto characteristics. Meanwhile, under the authorization of the shogunate, Tsuchimikado Yasufuku, influenced by the Tachikata Shintō, transformed Onmyōdō into what is known as Jinja Shintō. Before the Meiji era, retired Emperors conducting cloistered rule also occasionally performed the ritual of Shihōhai (worship in all four directions).{{sfn|小池康寿|2015|p=33}} {{sfn|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}} {{sfn|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}} {{sfn|小池康寿|2015|p=34}} {{sfn|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}} {{sfn|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}} {{sfn|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}} {{sfn|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}
In other bows made by the Emperor at Imperial Court ceremonies, the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|lt=regent|en}} or the head of the Shinto priest would sometimes bow on his behalf, but since the Shihohai was a bow to the Emperor's guardian star and parents, no bow was made on his behalf. In the "Kasetsu Ryakuki" written by [[:ja:白川雅喬|Masataka Shirakawa]] in the Edo period, he denies that Shihohai is a Shinto ritual, saying that it is a ritual to pay homage to guardian stars and ancestral shrines ("non-divine ritual"), so it is possible that Shihohai was a ritual established under [[Taoism]] or Onmyodo and was originally a ritual unrelated to Shinto {{sfn|村和明|2013}} .
Following the Emperor's example, [[Nobility|the nobles]] and commoners also performed Shihohai, praying for a good harvest and good health for the year {{NoteTag|『江家次第』には「関白四方拝」「庶臣儀」に関する記述もある{{要出典|date=2023rd year 12月}}。}}, but over time it came to remain only as an Imperial Court event {{NoteTag|ただし、江戸時代においても[[摂家]]など一部の公家の間でも四方拝が行われていた記録も残されている。例えば[[元文]]3rd year （[[1738]]）の元旦に当時の{{ill|Kanpaku|ja|関白|fr|Kanpaku|ru|Кампаку|sv|Kampaku|uk|Кампаку|zh|關白}}[[一条兼香]]が四方拝の行った時に記録が、彼の日記『兼香公記』に残されており、それによれば、天皇の四方拝と異なり三座が設けられず、山陵に代わって[[藤原氏]]や陰陽道に関わる諸神・諸社への拝礼が行われている{{要出典|date=2023rd year 12月}}。}} .
The festival was temporarily suspended during [[Ōnin War|the Onin War]] in the second half of [[15th century|the 15th century]], but was revived in [[Bunmei]] 7 ( [[1475]] ) during the reign of Emperor Go- Tsuchimikado, and was held in the front garden of the Seiryoden Hall of the Kyoto Imperial Palace until the reign of [[Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Komei]] in the second half of [[19th century|the 19th century]] .
== Edo Period == Subsequently, although the ceremony was interrupted with the [[Ōnin War|Onin War]], it started again in 1475, running from the reign of Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado to that of Emperor Komei; the ceremony was held in the front garden of the Palace of Heian (currently Kyoto Imperial Palace), Seiryo-den.<ref name="Yu" />
On January 1, torano koku (at about four o'clock in the morning), the Emperor, wearing Korozen no go-ho at Ryoki-den, came to the east garden of Seiryo-den and prayed for his Zokusho (one of the stars of the [[:en:Ursa_Major|Big Dipper]], which is said to have destiny depending on the year in which the person was born) and spirits in every direction, or the direction of his parents' {{ill|Japanese imperial tombs|lt=Imperial Mausoleum|fr|Tombes impériales japonaises|en}}, whereupon he wished for the peace and security of the nation and good harvests for the coming year.<ref name="Yu" />
The chanting words on this ceremony are described in '{{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Dairi (Japon)|lt=Dairi|fr|Dairi (Japon)|ja|内裏}} [https://www.japanesewiki.com/history/Gishiki%20(Book).html Gishiki]' and 'Go-ke Shidai.'<ref name="Yu" />
According to these materials, it is mentioned as Zokuko shichu kado ga shin, Dokuma shichu kado ga shin, Kiyaku shichu kado ga shin, Goki rokugai shichu kado ga shin, Hyakubyo joyu, Shoyoku zuishin, Kyukyu nyoritsu ryo.<ref name="Yu" />
== After the Meiji Period == After the Meiji period, from the viewpoint of {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Kokugaku|en}}, the influence of [[Taoism]] (belief in the Big Dipper and spells such as the Suiho-Ritsuryo system) was eliminated, and it was reconstructed as a Shinto ritual. It was held as a national event, called '''the Shiho-Setsu festival''', and was considered one of the four major festivals among national holidays.
After the Meiji period, it was regulated by Ordinance No. 1 of Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household), Koshitu Saishi Rei (Imperial Household Religious Rites) (1908). Prior to World War I, it was called Shiho-setsu and was conducted as a national ceremony, being considered one of the biggest of four major ceremonies held on national public holidays.<ref name="Yu" />
After the war, the ceremony was continued along with Koshitu Rei (Imperial Household) ordinance, although this law was eventually abolished.<ref name="Yu" />
After the war, the ceremony's name was changed to 'Shihohai' and it was conducted as a private function of the Imperial Family.<ref name="Yu" />
On January 1, at about 5:30 in the morning, the Emperor, wearing a traditional formal court dress called Korozen no go-ho, would enter a building constructed in the southern garden of Shinka-den, which is located west of the Three Shrines in the Imperial Court, whereupon he would bow toward the direction of two shrines--Ko-tai jingu Shrine and Toyouke Dai-jingu Shrine of Ise-jingu Shrine--and pray to spirits in various directions.<ref name="Yu" />
The Imperial mausoleums and Gods the Emperor prays for are, the Ise-jingu Shrine, Tenjin Chigi/all gods, Emperor Jimmu, former three Emperor's mausoleum (Fushimi Momoyama Imperial Mausoleum of Emperor Meiji, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Taisho, Musashi Imperial mausoleum of Emperor Showa), Ichi no miya Shrine in Musashi Province (Hikawa-jinja Shrine), Ichi no miya Shrine in Yamashiro Province (Kamowake ikazuchi-jinja Shrine and Kamo mioya-jinja Shrine), Iwashimizu Hachimangu Shrine, Atsuta-jingu Shrine, Kashima-jingu Shrine and Katori-jingu Shrine.<ref name="Yu" />
On New Year's Day in 1945, during World War II, air raid sirens sounded to warn of the impending attack of [[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|B-29 bombers]], but [[Hirohito|Emperor Showa]] used the Gobunko library, which was being used as an air raid shelter, as a makeshift funeral hall and performed a Shihohai ceremony. {{sfn|藤田尚徳|2015}}

{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Japanese Imperial Rituals}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of {{ill|January 1|ja|1月1日}} ({{ill|New Year's Day|ja|元日}}), in which the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|ja|天皇}} offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|deities|ja|神祇}}) in a {{ill|ceremony|ja|儀式}}. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅}} and for a bountiful harvest ({{ill|five grains|ja|五穀豊穣}}), making it part of the {{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this {{ill|Imperial Court rite|ja|宮中祭祀}} took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the {{ill|Imperial House|ja|皇室}}, carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|sokutai|ja|束帯}} called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿}} west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿}} in the {{ill|Kōkyo|ja|皇居}}. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮}} of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮}}, followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮}}, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇}} at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵}}, his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Taishō|ja|大正天皇}} at {{ill|Tama no Misasagi|ja|武蔵陵墓地}}, and his father, {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇}} at {{ill|Musashi Imperial Graveyard|ja|武蔵陵墓地}}.}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was {{ill|prayer for rain|ja|雨乞い}}, the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and {{ill|Fujiwara-kyō|ja|藤原京}} periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as {{ill|illness|ja|病気}}, {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病}}, {{ill|earthquakes|ja|地震}}, {{ill|fires|ja|火災}}, and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り}},” with the gods responsible personified as {{ill|oni|ja|鬼}} or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭}}, {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓}}, {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇}}’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the {{ill|Baekje no Omi|ja|百済王氏}}. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇}} (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor {{ill|Emperor Uda|ja|宇多天皇}} (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the {{ill|Uda Tennō Goki|ja|寛平御記}} entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉}}, there was a crackdown on {{ill|Onmyōji|ja|陰陽師}}, driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷}} and {{ill|fortune-telling|ja|占い}} into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)}} persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家}} of the {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道}} lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭}}) that centered on a specific {{ill|altar|ja|祭壇}}. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|ja|吉田神社}} in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教}} or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, {{ill|nobles|ja|貴族}} and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some {{ill|Kuge|ja|公家}} families, such as the {{ill|Sekke|ja|摂家}}, performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by {{ill|Ichijō Kaneka|ja|一条兼香}}, who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the {{ill|Ōnin War|ja|応仁の乱}} in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of {{ill|Bunmei (Japanese era)|ja|文明}} (1475) during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|ja|後土御門天皇}} and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿}} in the {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}} up through the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|ja|孝明天皇}} in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇}} donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星}} believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所}} and {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮}} from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|ja|後深草天皇}}, and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of {{ill|Kokugaku|ja|国学}}, elements considered to be derived from {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教}} (such as worshipping the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星}} guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿}} of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮}}—the {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇}}, the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇}} and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿}} (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機}}. Nevertheless, Emperor {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇}} carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *{{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀}} *{{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所}} *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間}} *{{ill|Saru-ga-tsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻}} [[Category:Imperial Household ceremonies]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Completion Tier 1]][[ja:四方拝]]
