revision.text:
{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of {{ill|January 1|ja|1月1日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|New Year's Day|ja|元日|12=draft|12=draft}}), in which the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|ja|天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|deities|ja|神祇|12=draft|12=draft}}) in a {{ill|ceremony|ja|儀式|12=draft|12=draft}}. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅|12=draft|12=draft}} and for a bountiful harvest ({{ill|five grains|ja|五穀豊穣|12=draft|12=draft}}), making it part of the {{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft|12=draft}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|12=draft|12=draft}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日|12=draft|12=draft}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this {{ill|Imperial Court rite|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|12=draft|12=draft}} took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令|12=draft|12=draft}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令|12=draft|12=draft}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the {{ill|Imperial House|ja|皇室|12=draft|12=draft}}, carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|sokutai|ja|束帯|12=draft|12=draft}} called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|12=draft|12=draft}} west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Kōkyo|ja|皇居|12=draft|12=draft}}. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神|12=draft|12=draft}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟|12=draft|12=draft}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|12=draft|12=draft}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵|12=draft|12=draft}}, his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Taishō|ja|大正天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} at {{ill|Tama no Misasagi|ja|武蔵陵墓地|12=draft|12=draft}}, and his father, {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} at {{ill|Musashi Imperial Graveyard|ja|武蔵陵墓地|12=draft|12=draft}}.}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所|12=draft|12=draft}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft|12=draft}}, under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was {{ill|prayer for rain|ja|雨乞い|12=draft|12=draft}}, the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and {{ill|Fujiwara-kyō|ja|藤原京|12=draft|12=draft}} periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳|12=draft|12=draft}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as {{ill|illness|ja|病気|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|earthquakes|ja|地震|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|fires|ja|火災|12=draft|12=draft}}, and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災|12=draft|12=draft}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り|12=draft|12=draft}},” with the gods responsible personified as {{ill|oni|ja|鬼|12=draft|12=draft}} or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神|12=draft|12=draft}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft}} had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀|12=draft|12=draft}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|12=draft|12=draft}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|12=draft|12=draft}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the {{ill|Baekje no Omi|ja|百済王氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor {{ill|Emperor Uda|ja|宇多天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the {{ill|Uda Tennō Goki|ja|寛平御記|12=draft|12=draft}} entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝|12=draft|12=draft}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|12=draft|12=draft}}, there was a crackdown on {{ill|Onmyōji|ja|陰陽師|12=draft|12=draft}}, driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|fortune-telling|ja|占い|12=draft|12=draft}} into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|12=draft|12=draft}} persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft}} lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭|12=draft|12=draft}}) that centered on a specific {{ill|altar|ja|祭壇|12=draft|12=draft}}. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|ja|吉田神社|12=draft|12=draft}} in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福|12=draft|12=draft}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関|12=draft|12=draft}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯|12=draft|12=draft}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記|12=draft|12=draft}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬|12=draft|12=draft}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教|12=draft|12=draft}} or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, {{ill|nobles|ja|貴族|12=draft|12=draft}} and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some {{ill|Kuge|ja|公家|12=draft|12=draft}} families, such as the {{ill|Sekke|ja|摂家|12=draft|12=draft}}, performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by {{ill|Ichijō Kaneka|ja|一条兼香|12=draft|12=draft}}, who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白|12=draft|12=draft}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏|12=draft|12=draft}} and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the {{ill|Ōnin War|ja|応仁の乱|12=draft|12=draft}} in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of {{ill|Bunmei (Japanese era)|ja|文明|12=draft|12=draft}} (1475) during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|ja|後土御門天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所|12=draft|12=draft}} up through the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|ja|孝明天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所|12=draft|12=draft}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|12=draft|12=draft}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星|12=draft|12=draft}} believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院|12=draft|12=draft}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|ja|後深草天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}, and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式|12=draft|12=draft}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第|12=draft|12=draft}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀|12=draft|12=draft}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令|12=draft|12=draft}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of {{ill|Kokugaku|ja|国学|12=draft|12=draft}}, elements considered to be derived from {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教|12=draft|12=draft}} (such as worshipping the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星|12=draft|12=draft}} guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|12=draft|12=draft}} ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|12=draft|12=draft}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長|12=draft|12=draft}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}—the {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇|12=draft|12=draft}}, the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|12=draft|12=draft}} (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機|12=draft|12=draft}}. Nevertheless, Emperor {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫|12=draft|12=draft}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *{{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Saru-ga-tsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻|12=draft|12=draft}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:New]] }} [[ja:四方拝]] [[sn:Shihohai]]

{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of {{ill|January 1|ja|1月1日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|New Year's Day|ja|元日|12=draft|12=draft}}), in which the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|ja|天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|deities|ja|神祇|12=draft|12=draft}}) in a {{ill|ceremony|ja|儀式|12=draft|12=draft}}. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅|12=draft|12=draft}} and for a bountiful harvest ({{ill|five grains|ja|五穀豊穣|12=draft|12=draft}}), making it part of the {{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|12=draft|12=draft}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|12=draft|12=draft}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日|12=draft|12=draft}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this {{ill|Imperial Court rite|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|12=draft|12=draft}} took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令|12=draft|12=draft}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令|12=draft|12=draft}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the {{ill|Imperial House|ja|皇室|12=draft|12=draft}}, carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|sokutai|ja|束帯|12=draft|12=draft}} called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|12=draft|12=draft}} west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Kōkyo|ja|皇居|12=draft|12=draft}}. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神|12=draft|12=draft}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟|12=draft|12=draft}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|12=draft|12=draft}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵|12=draft|12=draft}}, his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Taishō|ja|大正天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} at {{ill|Tama no Misasagi|ja|武蔵陵墓地|12=draft|12=draft}}, and his father, {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} at {{ill|Musashi Imperial Graveyard|ja|武蔵陵墓地|12=draft|12=draft}}.}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所|12=draft|12=draft}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft|12=draft}}, under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was {{ill|prayer for rain|ja|雨乞い|12=draft|12=draft}}, the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and {{ill|Fujiwara-kyō|ja|藤原京|12=draft|12=draft}} periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳|12=draft|12=draft}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as {{ill|illness|ja|病気|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|earthquakes|ja|地震|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|fires|ja|火災|12=draft|12=draft}}, and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災|12=draft|12=draft}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り|12=draft|12=draft}},” with the gods responsible personified as {{ill|oni|ja|鬼|12=draft|12=draft}} or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神|12=draft|12=draft}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft}} had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀|12=draft|12=draft}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭|12=draft|12=draft}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|12=draft|12=draft}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|12=draft|12=draft}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the {{ill|Baekje no Omi|ja|百済王氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor {{ill|Emperor Uda|ja|宇多天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the {{ill|Uda Tennō Goki|ja|寛平御記|12=draft|12=draft}} entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝|12=draft|12=draft}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|12=draft|12=draft}}, there was a crackdown on {{ill|Onmyōji|ja|陰陽師|12=draft|12=draft}}, driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|fortune-telling|ja|占い|12=draft|12=draft}} into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|12=draft|12=draft}} persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft}} lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭|12=draft|12=draft}}) that centered on a specific {{ill|altar|ja|祭壇|12=draft|12=draft}}. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|ja|吉田神社|12=draft|12=draft}} in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福|12=draft|12=draft}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関|12=draft|12=draft}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯|12=draft|12=draft}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記|12=draft|12=draft}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬|12=draft|12=draft}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教|12=draft|12=draft}} or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, {{ill|nobles|ja|貴族|12=draft|12=draft}} and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some {{ill|Kuge|ja|公家|12=draft|12=draft}} families, such as the {{ill|Sekke|ja|摂家|12=draft|12=draft}}, performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by {{ill|Ichijō Kaneka|ja|一条兼香|12=draft|12=draft}}, who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白|12=draft|12=draft}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏|12=draft|12=draft}} and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the {{ill|Ōnin War|ja|応仁の乱|12=draft|12=draft}} in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of {{ill|Bunmei (Japanese era)|ja|文明|12=draft|12=draft}} (1475) during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|ja|後土御門天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所|12=draft|12=draft}} up through the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|ja|孝明天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所|12=draft|12=draft}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|12=draft|12=draft}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星|12=draft|12=draft}} believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院|12=draft|12=draft}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|ja|後深草天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}, and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式|12=draft|12=draft}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第|12=draft|12=draft}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀|12=draft|12=draft}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令|12=draft|12=draft}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of {{ill|Kokugaku|ja|国学|12=draft|12=draft}}, elements considered to be derived from {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教|12=draft|12=draft}} (such as worshipping the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星|12=draft|12=draft}} guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|12=draft|12=draft}} ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|12=draft|12=draft}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|12=draft|12=draft}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長|12=draft|12=draft}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}—the {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇|12=draft|12=draft}}, the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社|12=draft|12=draft}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|12=draft|12=draft}} (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機|12=draft|12=draft}}. Nevertheless, Emperor {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇|12=draft|12=draft}} carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫|12=draft|12=draft}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *{{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間|12=draft|12=draft}} *{{ill|Saru-ga-tsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻|12=draft|12=draft}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:New]] }} [[ja:四方拝]] [[sn:Shihohai]]

{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of {{ill|January 1|ja|1月1日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|New Year's Day|ja|元日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), in which the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|deities|ja|神祇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in a {{ill|ceremony|ja|儀式|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and for a bountiful harvest ({{ill|five grains|ja|五穀豊穣|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), making it part of the {{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this {{ill|Imperial Court rite|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|qq=draft|qq=draft}} took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the {{ill|Imperial House|ja|皇室|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|sokutai|ja|束帯|qq=draft|qq=draft}} called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} west of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Kōkyo|ja|皇居|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Taishō|ja|大正天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Tama no Misasagi|ja|武蔵陵墓地|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and his father, {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Musashi Imperial Graveyard|ja|武蔵陵墓地|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was {{ill|prayer for rain|ja|雨乞い|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and {{ill|Fujiwara-kyō|ja|藤原京|qq=draft|qq=draft}} periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as {{ill|illness|ja|病気|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|earthquakes|ja|地震|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|fires|ja|火災|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” with the gods responsible personified as {{ill|oni|ja|鬼|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Ōharae|ja|大祓|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the {{ill|Baekje no Omi|ja|百済王氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor {{ill|Emperor Uda|ja|宇多天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the {{ill|Uda Tennō Goki|ja|寛平御記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, there was a crackdown on {{ill|Onmyōji|ja|陰陽師|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|fortune-telling|ja|占い|qq=draft|qq=draft}} into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) that centered on a specific {{ill|altar|ja|祭壇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|ja|吉田神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福|qq=draft|qq=draft}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬|qq=draft|qq=draft}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, {{ill|nobles|ja|貴族|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some {{ill|Kuge|ja|公家|qq=draft|qq=draft}} families, such as the {{ill|Sekke|ja|摂家|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by {{ill|Ichijō Kaneka|ja|一条兼香|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the {{ill|Ōnin War|ja|応仁の乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of {{ill|Bunmei (Japanese era)|ja|文明|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (1475) during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|ja|後土御門天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所|qq=draft|qq=draft}} up through the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|ja|孝明天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星|qq=draft|qq=draft}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星|qq=draft|qq=draft}} believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Go-Fukakusa|ja|後深草天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令|qq=draft|qq=draft}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of {{ill|Kokugaku|ja|国学|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, elements considered to be derived from {{ill|Taoism|ja|道教|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (such as worshipping the {{ill|Big Dipper|ja|北斗七星|qq=draft|qq=draft}} guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—the {{ill|Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ({{ill|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine|ja|賀茂別雷神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Kamo Mizuo Shrine|ja|賀茂御祖神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|ja|石清水八幡宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|ja|熱田神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|ja|宮中三殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Nevertheless, Emperor {{ill|Emperor Shōwa|ja|昭和天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *{{ill|Imperial Court rites|ja|宮中祭祀|1=Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|lt=Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace|qq=draft|qq=draft}} *{{ill|Kyoto Imperial Palace|ja|京都御所|qq=draft|qq=draft}} *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間|qq=draft|qq=draft}} *{{ill|Saru-ga-tsuji|ja|猿ヶ辻|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:New]] }} [[ja:四方拝]] [[sn:Shihohai]]

{{複数の問題|出典の明記=2017年8月28日 (月) 07:48 (UTC)|独自研究=2017年8月28日 (月) 07:48 (UTC)}} [[ファイル:Shihouhai.jpg|サムネイル|[[清涼殿]]前庭での四方拝（「近代年中行事絵」）]] {{皇室祭祀}} '''四方拝'''（しほうはい）とは、毎年[[1月1日]]（[[元日]]）の早朝、宮中の庭で[[天皇]]が天地四方の[[神祇]]を拝する[[儀式]]。四方を拝し、[[年災消滅]]、[[五穀豊穣]]を祈る[[宮中祭祀]]{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}。 == 概要 == 四方拜は、毎年1月1日（元日）の早朝、[[歳旦祭]]に先だって、宮中・[[神嘉殿]]の南庭で天皇が天地四方の神祇を拝する儀式である。殿上ではなく庭上で行われるのは天皇自らが地上に降り立ち身をへり下り天神地祇を拝するという意味があるとされ、このことを「'''庭上下御'''」という{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}。 [[祝祭日]]が法定された明治時代初期から[[1945年]]（昭和20年）頃までは、この[[宮中祭祀]]の行われる1月1日は'''四方節'''とよばれていた。[[皇室令]]の一つである[[皇室祭祀令]]（明治41年皇室令第1号）第23条は、「歳旦祭ノ当日ニハ之ニ先タチ四方拝ノ式ヲ行ヒ…但シ天皇喪ニ在リ其ノ他事故アルトキハ四方拝ノ式ヲ行ハス」と定める。[[1947年]]（昭和22年）に同令が廃止された後は、[[皇室]]の私的な行事として、旧例に準拠して行われている。 儀式の大要は次の通りである。1月1日（元日）の午前5時30分に、天皇が[[黄櫨染御袍]]と呼ばれる[[束帯]]を着用し、[[皇居]]の[[宮中三殿]]の西側にある神嘉殿の南側の庭に設けられた仮屋の中に入り、[[伊勢神宮]]の[[皇大神宮]]・[[豊受大神宮]]の両宮に向かって拝礼した後、続いて四方の諸神祇を拝する。この時に天皇が拝する神々・天皇陵は、[[伊勢神宮]]、[[天津神・国津神|天神地祇]]、[[神武天皇#陵・霊廟|神武天皇陵]]・先帝三代の各山陵{{Efn2|[[上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|上皇]][[明仁]]の場合、曾祖父・[[明治天皇]]の[[伏見桃山陵]]、祖父・[[大正天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|多摩陵]]、父・[[昭和天皇]]の[[武蔵陵墓地|武蔵野陵]]の三陵。}}、[[武蔵国]][[一宮]]（[[氷川神社]]）、[[山城国]]一宮（[[賀茂別雷神社]]と[[賀茂御祖神社]]）、[[石清水八幡宮]]、[[熱田神宮]]、[[常陸国]][[一宮]]（[[鹿島神宮]]）、[[下総国]][[一宮]]（[[香取神宮]]）である。 [[2009年]]（平成21年）の四方拝は、当時の天皇[[明仁]]（第125代天皇）の高齢化に伴う祭祀の簡略化により、皇居の[[御所]]において行われた。 == 沿革 == ===草創期から江戸時代末期まで=== === 飛鳥時代 === 本朝における四方拝の文献上の初見は、『[[日本書紀]]』の「[[皇極天皇]]元年八月朔日条」である{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}。天皇は南渕で「四方を拝み、天を仰ぎ祈り給ふ」と出ており、これがそもそもの始まりだという{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}。この時の皇極天皇の四方拝は[[雨乞い|祈雨]]が目的であったが、天皇の親拝であること、その名称が「四方拝」であることから、平安期に制度化した四方拝への何らかの影響関係があるとされている{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|皇極天皇の漢風諡号の「皇極」と重祚した時の「斉明」は中国古典に由来するが共に「中央」や北斗七星と関連がある語である{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}。}}。 また飛鳥・[[藤原京]]時代の天皇陵は[[八角墳]]であり、大極殿の高御座も八角形につくられていることなどから、藤原京では四方八方の全土の支配と安寧をしめす祭儀が行われていたと考えられる{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}。このようなことから、代拝不可の要素は北辰を拝する天皇の大権に関わる可能性もあるとされている{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}。 === 平安時代 === [[病気]]や[[疫病]]、[[地震]]、[[火災]]、[[天災]]といった災い事は、すべて「[[神]]の[[祟り]]が起こすもの」と考えられ、[[祟り]]を起こす[[神]]の存在を[[鬼]]に例えたり、[[疫神]]として恐れていた{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}。[[陰陽道]]が平安貴族社会を基盤にして[[呪術]]的に展開されており、[[律令制]]の[[神祇祭祀]]の中に、陰陽要素を含む祭祀が数多く存在し{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}、[[疫神祭]]、[[鎮花祭]]、[[風神祭]]、[[大祓]]、[[宮城四隅疫神祭]]、[[防解火災祭]]、[[螢惑星祭]]など様々な、祭祀が行われており{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}、京内を結界（聖なる領域と俗なる領域）し、[[京城四隅疫神祭]]（都）や[[宮城四隅疫神祭]]（内裏）など、「四角四境」の祭祀を行い、世の安泰を願っていた{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}。 平安期の四方拝制度化には[[桓武天皇]]が行った古代中国の皇帝祭祀である[[郊祀]]の影響が見られるとされる。これは古代中国の皇帝が行っていた祭天郊祀を朝鮮半島で唯一行っていた[[百済王]]（冊封候である新羅・高句麗は皇帝を憚って郊祀をしなかった）より[[百済王氏]]を通じてその支援の下に行われたものであったとされる{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}。 現在行われている四方拝は[[平安時代]]初期、[[嵯峨天皇]]の治世（[[9世紀]]初め）に宮中で始まったとされている。儀式として定着したのは[[宇多天皇]]の時代（9世紀末）とされ、『[[寛平御記|宇多天皇御記]]』の[[寛平]]2年[[1月1日 (旧暦)|元旦]]（[[ユリウス暦]][[890年]]1月25日）が四方拝が行われた最古の記録である。 宇多天皇は「わが国は神国である。よって毎朝四方の大中小の神祇を敬拝する。敬拝のことは、今より始まる。以後一日たりとも怠ること無し」（『宇多天皇御記』仁和四年十月十九日条）と記してあり、嵯峨天皇の弘仁年間に成立した「元旦四方拝」を前提にその制度化と「[[毎朝御拝]]」の創祀があったと考えられている{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}。 === 安土桃山時代 === [[豊臣秀吉]]による[[陰陽師]][[弾圧]]や[[迫害]]が始まり、[[祈祷]]や[[占い]]を[[生業]]とする陰陽師を地方に追いやり、一気に力を失っていき、当時[[陰陽寮]]にいた正式な陰陽師の数をはるかに超える陰陽師と名乗る人間が全国に流れた{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}。[[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]の[[迫害]]で、筆頭の[[土御門家]]であっても[[陰陽道]]の[[相伝]]や[[法具]]などの多くを焼失した。陰陽道の最も重要な「[[大法]]」の[[泰山府君]]祭（たいざんふくんさい）の[[祭壇]]も喪失し、[[京都]][[吉田神社]]から法具を借用して[[御所]]の地鎮祭を行った。その影響が大きく、宮中祭祀は神道色を色濃くしていった{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}。一方陰陽道は、[[江戸幕府|幕府]]からの認可のもと、[[土御門泰福]]が[[垂加神道]]の影響を受けて[[天社神道]]として神道化させた{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}} 宮中祭祀において天皇が行う他の拝礼では、[[摂関]]や[[神祇伯]]が代拝することもあったが、四方拝は天皇本人の守護星や父母に対する拝礼であるため、代拝は行われなかった。江戸時代に[[白川雅喬]]が著した『家説略記』には、四方拝は守護星・祖廟を拝礼する儀式であると述べて神道儀礼であることを否定している（「非神祭」）ことから、四方拝が[[道教]]や[[陰陽道]]の下に成立した儀式であって、本来神道とは無関係な儀式であった可能性もある{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}。 天皇に倣って、[[貴族]]や庶民の間でも四方拜は行われ、一年間の豊作と無病息災を祈ったが{{Efn2|『江家次第』には「関白四方拝」「庶臣儀」に関する記述もある{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}}、時代を経るごとに宮中行事として残るのみとなった{{Efn2|ただし、江戸時代においても[[摂家]]など一部の公家の間でも四方拝が行われていた記録も残されている。例えば[[元文]]3年（[[1738年]]）の元旦に当時の[[関白]][[一条兼香]]が四方拝の行った時に記録が、彼の日記『兼香公記』に残されており、それによれば、天皇の四方拝と異なり三座が設けられず、山陵に代わって[[藤原氏]]や陰陽道に関わる諸神・諸社への拝礼が行われている{{要出典|date=2023年12月}}。}}。 [[15世紀]]後半には[[応仁の乱]]で一時中断されたが、[[後土御門天皇]]の治世の[[文明_(日本)|文明]]7年（[[1475年]]）に再興されて以後、[[19世紀]]後半の[[孝明天皇]]の治世に至るまで、[[京都御所]]の[[清涼殿]]の前庭で行われた。 ===明治以前の式次第=== 1月1日の[[寅]]の刻（午前4時ごろ）に、[[天皇]]が[[御所]]の[[綾綺殿]]で[[黄櫨染御袍]]を着用し、[[清涼殿]]東庭に出御する。清涼殿東庭には、あらかじめ、「嘱星御拝御座」「四方御拝御座」「山陵御拝御座」の'''三座'''が設けられている。 天皇はまず最初に「嘱星御拝御座」に着座して、天皇の属星（ぞくしょう）{{Efn2|属星（ぞくしょう）とは、誕生年によって定まるという人間の運命を司る[[北斗七星]]のなかの星のことで、子年は貪狼星（ドゥーベ）、丑年と亥年は巨門星（メラク）、寅年と戌年は禄存星（フェクダ）、卯年と酉年は文曲星（メグレズ）、辰年と申年は廉貞星（アリオト）、巳年と未年は武曲星（ミザール）、午年は破軍星（アルカイド、ベネトナシュ）となる{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}。}}に拝礼する。次に「四方御拝御座」に着座して天地四方の神霊に拝礼する。最後に「山陵御拝御座」に着座して父母の山陵（父母が健在の場合には省略）などの方向を拝礼する。それぞれ、玉体安穏・宝祚延長を祈った。また、江戸時代には、属星拝礼後に「嘱星御拝御座」において[[内侍所]]・[[伊勢神宮]]への拝礼が行われ、父母の御陵拝礼前に「山陵御拝御座」にて歴代天皇の山陵（対象は時期によって異なる）に対する拝礼が追加されたことも知られている。なお、伊勢神宮への拝礼に関しては院四方拝においては、[[後深草天皇|後深草院]]以来の慣例であったとする『[[花園天皇日記]]』[[元応]]2年（[[1320年]]）元日条の記事があり、中世に院で行われたものが後に天皇の四方拝でも採用されたと考えられている。 この拝礼のとき、天皇は独特の言葉（呪文）を唱えた。それは『[[内裏儀式]]』・『[[江家次第]]』によると次の通りである。 {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} なお、「五危」は「五厄」とする史料もある。 また明治時代以前の元旦四方拝の祭器具には「'''大宋御屏風'''」があったが、「大宋」とは中国南朝の「[[劉宋]]」のことであり、漢の天地を祭る皇帝祭祀である明堂祭祀が南朝の劉宋を経て日本に継承された品であると位置づけられること、元旦四方拝の天皇の礼服である[[黄櫨染御袍]]は「[[月令]]思想」の中央である土王「黄」を表しているとし古代中国の皇帝祭祀との関連も指摘されている{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}。 『内裏儀式』『西宮記』によれば正月元旦、鶏鳴の丑刻（午前二時）より東庭に屏風四帖が立てられ、属星を拝する座の前には燈明、各座の前には白木の机の上に香が焚かれ花が置かれ、寅の刻（午前三時）から行われてきた。祭儀次第は一、属星拝。二、天地四方拝。三、（父母）二陵拝。であったという{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}。 ===明治時代以後=== 明治以後は、[[国学]]的観点から、[[道教]]の影響（[[北斗七星]]信仰や急々如律令などの呪文）は排除され、神道祭祀として再構成された上、国の行事として行われて'''四方節'''と呼ばれ、祝祭日の中の四大節の一つとされていた。 ;明治時代以後の式次第 :式に先だって、皇居・宮中三殿の付属施設である神嘉殿の南庭にあらかじめ仮屋を設け、中央に[[簾薦]]を敷き[[屏風]]2双を立ち廻らし、その中に御座を設け[[灯台 (照明器具)|灯台]]2基を供する。1月1日午前5時30分、天皇は[[綾綺殿]]で[[黄櫨染御袍]]を着用し、[[掌典長]]の先導で神嘉殿南庭に出る。拝礼の御座で、[[伊勢神宮]]の[[皇大神宮]]・[[豊受大神宮]]の両宮に向かって拝礼した後、続いて四方の諸神祇を拝する。この時に天皇が拝する神々・天皇陵は、[[伊勢神宮]]、[[天神地祇]]、[[神武天皇|神武天皇陵]]・先帝三代の各山陵、[[武蔵国]][[一宮]]（[[氷川神社]]）、[[山城国]]一宮（[[賀茂別雷神社]]と[[賀茂御祖神社]]）、[[石清水八幡宮]]、[[熱田神宮]]、[[常陸国]][[一宮]]（[[鹿島神宮]]）、[[下総国]][[一宮]]（[[香取神宮]]）でこれらを順次拝する。四方拝を終えると、天皇は[[宮中三殿]]（賢所、皇霊殿、神殿）をそれぞれ拝礼する。 :天皇に事故があって四方拝を行えないときも代拝を行わない慣例は、従前の通りである。 第二次世界大戦中の昭和20年（1945）の元旦には、[[B29爆撃機]]の襲来を知らせる空襲警報が鳴ったが、[[昭和天皇]]は防空壕としていた[[御文庫]]前を臨時の斎場として四方拝を執り行った{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}。 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === 注釈 ===
