{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of [[:en:January 1|January 1]] ([[:en:New Year's Day|New Year's Day]]), in which the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]] offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Deities|ja|神祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/deities|qq=}}) in a [[:en:Ritual|ceremony]]. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/elimination of annual calamities|qq=}} and for a bountiful harvest ([[:en:Bumper crop|five grains]]), making it part of the [[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinka-den|qq=}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/national holidays|qq=}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this [[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]] took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House observances ordinance|qq=}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House ordinances|qq=}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]], carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the [[:en:Sokutai|sokutai]] called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinka-den|qq=}} west of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] in the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Kōkyo]]. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtaijingū|qq=}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōyuke Daijingū|qq=}} of the [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]], followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]], {{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|qq=}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Jimmu|qq=}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōkō|qq=}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|qq=}}, his grandfather, [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] at [[:en:Musashi Imperial Graveyard|Tama no Misasagi]], and his father, [[:en:Hirohito|Emperor Shōwa]] at [[:en:Musashi Imperial Graveyard|Musashi Imperial Graveyard]].}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|qq=}} ([[:en:Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]]), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ([[:en:Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[:en:Shimogamo Shrine|Kamo Mizuo Shrine]]), [[:en:Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachimangū]], [[:en:Atsuta Shrine|Atsuta Shrine]], Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ([[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Shrine]]), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ([[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]]). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gosho|qq=}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Empress Kōgyoku|qq=}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was [[:en:Rainmaking (ritual)|prayer for rain]], the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and [[:en:Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyō]] periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/eight-lobed tumuli|qq=}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as [[:en:Disease|illness]], {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/epidemics|qq=}}, [[:en:Earthquake|earthquakes]], [[:en:Conflagration|fires]], and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/natural disasters|qq=}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/wrath of gods|qq=}},” with the gods responsible personified as [[:en:Oni|oni]] or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/epidemic deities|qq=}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|qq=}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ekishin-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinka-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūjin-sai|qq=}}, [[:en:Ōharae-shiki|Ōharae]], {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bōke kasai-sai|qq=}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keiwakusei-sai|qq=}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|qq=}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]]’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jisa|13=User:Immanuelle/Jiao Sacrifices|qq=}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the [[:en:Kudara no Konikishi clan|Baekje no Omi]]. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Saga|Emperor Saga]] (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor [[:en:Emperor Uda|Emperor Uda]] (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the [[:en:Kanpyō Gyoki|Uda Tennō Goki]] entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maichō Gohai|qq=}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]], there was a crackdown on [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]], driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/incantations|qq=}} and [[:en:Divination|fortune-telling]] into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the [[:en:Sengoku period|Sengoku period]] persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} of the [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tai-san fukun-sai|qq=}}) that centered on a specific [[:en:Altar|altar]]. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the [[:en:Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]] in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|qq=}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Torigoe Shintō|qq=}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sesshō and Kampaku|qq=}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jingi-haku|qq=}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iesetsu ryakuki|qq=}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|qq=}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of [[:en:Taoism|Taoism]] or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, [[:en:Nobility|nobles]] and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some [[:en:Kuge|Kuge]] families, such as the [[:en:Five regent houses|Five regent houses]], performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by [[:en:Ichijō Kaneka|Ichijō Kaneka]], who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kampaku|qq=}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the [[:en:Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara clan]] and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of [[:en:Civilization|Bunmei (Japanese era)]] (1475) during the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado]] and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}} in the [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] up through the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Kōmei]] in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor]] donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayahashidono|qq=}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|qq=}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zokushō|qq=}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the [[:en:Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishidokoro|qq=}} and [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]] from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nyoin|qq=}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Fukakusa|Emperor Go-Fukakusa]], and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naidairi Gishiki|qq=}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eke Shidai|qq=}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ming tang sacrifice|qq=}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yueling|qq=}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of [[:en:Kokugaku|Kokugaku]], elements considered to be derived from [[:en:Taoism|Taoism]] (such as worshipping the [[:en:Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayahashidono|qq=}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|qq=}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]]—the {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtaijingū|qq=}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōyuke Daijingū|qq=}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|qq=}}, the mausoleum of [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|qq=}} ([[:en:Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]]), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ([[:en:Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[:en:Shimogamo Shrine|Kamo Mizuo Shrine]]), [[:en:Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachimangū]], [[:en:Atsuta Shrine|Atsuta Shrine]], Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ([[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Shrine]]), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ([[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]]). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/B-29 bombers|qq=}}. Nevertheless, Emperor [[:en:Hirohito|Emperor Shōwa]] carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/O-bunko|qq=}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *[[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]] *[[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oni no Ma|qq=}} *[[:en:Sarugatsuji|Saru-ga-tsuji]] {{Shinto-stub}} {{translated page|ja|四方拝|version=104519723|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Shihohai]][[Category:qq]] }} [[ja:四方拝]] [[sn:Shihohai]]

revision.text:
{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of [[:en:January 1|January 1]] ([[:en:New Year's Day|New Year's Day]]), in which the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]] offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Deities|ja|神祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/deities|qq=}}) in a [[:en:Ritual|ceremony]]. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/elimination of annual calamities|qq=}} and for a bountiful harvest ([[:en:Bumper crop|five grains]]), making it part of the [[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinka-den|qq=}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/national holidays|qq=}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this [[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]] took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House observances ordinance|qq=}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House ordinances|qq=}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]], carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the [[:en:Sokutai|sokutai]] called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinka-den|qq=}} west of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] in the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Kōkyo]]. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtaijingū|qq=}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōyuke Daijingū|qq=}} of the [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]], followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]], {{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|qq=}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Jimmu|qq=}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōkō|qq=}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|qq=}}, his grandfather, [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] at [[:en:Musashi Imperial Graveyard|Tama no Misasagi]], and his father, [[:en:Hirohito|Emperor Shōwa]] at [[:en:Musashi Imperial Graveyard|Musashi Imperial Graveyard]].}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|qq=}} ([[:en:Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]]), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ([[:en:Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[:en:Shimogamo Shrine|Kamo Mizuo Shrine]]), [[:en:Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachimangū]], [[:en:Atsuta Shrine|Atsuta Shrine]], Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ([[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Shrine]]), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ([[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]]). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gosho|qq=}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Empress Kōgyoku|qq=}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was [[:en:Rainmaking (ritual)|prayer for rain]], the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and [[:en:Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyō]] periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/eight-lobed tumuli|qq=}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as [[:en:Disease|illness]], {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/epidemics|qq=}}, [[:en:Earthquake|earthquakes]], [[:en:Conflagration|fires]], and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/natural disasters|qq=}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/wrath of gods|qq=}},” with the gods responsible personified as [[:en:Oni|oni]] or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/epidemic deities|qq=}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|qq=}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ekishin-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinka-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūjin-sai|qq=}}, [[:en:Ōharae-shiki|Ōharae]], {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bōke kasai-sai|qq=}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keiwakusei-sai|qq=}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|qq=}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]]’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jisa|13=User:Immanuelle/Jiao Sacrifices|qq=}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the [[:en:Kudara no Konikishi clan|Baekje no Omi]]. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Saga|Emperor Saga]] (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor [[:en:Emperor Uda|Emperor Uda]] (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the [[:en:Kanpyō Gyoki|Uda Tennō Goki]] entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maichō Gohai|qq=}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]], there was a crackdown on [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]], driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/incantations|qq=}} and [[:en:Divination|fortune-telling]] into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the [[:en:Sengoku period|Sengoku period]] persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} of the [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tai-san fukun-sai|qq=}}) that centered on a specific [[:en:Altar|altar]]. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the [[:en:Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]] in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|qq=}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Torigoe Shintō|qq=}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sesshō and Kampaku|qq=}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jingi-haku|qq=}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iesetsu ryakuki|qq=}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|qq=}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of [[:en:Taoism|Taoism]] or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, [[:en:Nobility|nobles]] and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some [[:en:Kuge|Kuge]] families, such as the [[:en:Five regent houses|Five regent houses]], performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by [[:en:Ichijō Kaneka|Ichijō Kaneka]], who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kampaku|qq=}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the [[:en:Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara clan]] and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of [[:en:Civilization|Bunmei (Japanese era)]] (1475) during the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado]] and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}} in the [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] up through the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Kōmei]] in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor]] donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayahashidono|qq=}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|qq=}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zokushō|qq=}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the [[:en:Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishidokoro|qq=}} and [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]] from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nyoin|qq=}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Fukakusa|Emperor Go-Fukakusa]], and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naidairi Gishiki|qq=}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eke Shidai|qq=}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ming tang sacrifice|qq=}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yueling|qq=}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of [[:en:Kokugaku|Kokugaku]], elements considered to be derived from [[:en:Taoism|Taoism]] (such as worshipping the [[:en:Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayahashidono|qq=}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|qq=}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]]—the {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtaijingū|qq=}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōyuke Daijingū|qq=}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|qq=}}, the mausoleum of [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|qq=}} ([[:en:Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]]), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ([[:en:Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[:en:Shimogamo Shrine|Kamo Mizuo Shrine]]), [[:en:Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachimangū]], [[:en:Atsuta Shrine|Atsuta Shrine]], Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ([[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Shrine]]), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ([[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]]). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/B-29 bombers|qq=}}. Nevertheless, Emperor [[:en:Hirohito|Emperor Shōwa]] carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/O-bunko|qq=}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *[[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]] *[[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oni no Ma|qq=}} *[[:en:Sarugatsuji|Saru-ga-tsuji]] {{Shinto-stub}} {{translated page|ja|四方拝|version=104519723|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Shihohai]][[Category:qq]] }} [[ja:四方拝]] [[sn:Shihohai]] [[Category:新春の季語]]

{{Multiple issues |needs references=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) |original research=August 28, 2017 (Mon) 07:48 (UTC) }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Shihōhai''' (四方拝) is a yearly ritual performed in the early morning of [[:en:January 1|January 1]] ([[:en:New Year's Day|New Year's Day]]), in which the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]] offers worship to the deities of heaven and earth in all four directions ({{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Deities|ja|神祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/deities|qq=}}) in a [[:en:Ritual|ceremony]]. By bowing in the four directions, prayers are offered for the {{ill|elimination of annual calamities|ja|年災消滅|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/elimination of annual calamities|qq=}} and for a bountiful harvest ([[:en:Bumper crop|five grains]]), making it part of the [[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52-53}}. == Overview == Shihōhai is a ritual performed in the early morning of January 1 (New Year’s Day) before the {{ill|Saitan-sai|ja|歳旦祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saitan-sai|qq=}}. In the southern courtyard of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinka-den|qq=}} within the Imperial Court, the Emperor worships the deities of heaven and earth in the four directions. It is said that performing it in the courtyard—rather than on an elevated palace platform—conveys that the Emperor himself steps down to ground level to humble himself in worship of the celestial and terrestrial gods, an act referred to as “'''Nyajōgego''' (庭上下御)”{{Sfnp|松山能夫|1966|pp=75-76}}. From the early Meiji period, when {{ill|national holidays|ja|祝祭日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/national holidays|qq=}} were codified, until around 1945 (Shōwa 20), January 1—when this [[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]] took place—was called “'''Shihōsetsu'''.” Article 23 of the {{ill|Imperial House observances ordinance|ja|皇室祭祀令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House observances ordinance|qq=}} (Imperial House Ordinance No. 1 of Meiji 41), one of the {{ill|Imperial House ordinances|ja|皇室令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House ordinances|qq=}}, stipulates: “On the day of the Saitan-sai, the Ceremony of Shihōhai is conducted beforehand… However, if the Emperor is in mourning or if other circumstances arise, the Shihōhai Ceremony will not be performed.” After the repeal of that ordinance in 1947 (Shōwa 22), the ceremony continued as a private event of the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]], carried out in accordance with former practice. The main outline of the ceremony is as follows: At 5:30 a.m. on January 1 (New Year’s Day), the Emperor dresses in the [[:en:Sokutai|sokutai]] called {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}}, then proceeds to a temporary shelter set up on the south side of the {{ill|Shinka-den|ja|神嘉殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinka-den|qq=}} west of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] in the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Kōkyo]]. There, he first offers worship facing the two shrines of {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtaijingū|qq=}} and {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōyuke Daijingū|qq=}} of the [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]], followed by worship of various deities of the four directions. The gods and Imperial mausoleums worshipped by the Emperor at this time are: [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]], {{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天津神・国津神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|qq=}} (the celestial and terrestrial deities), the mausoleum of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇#陵・霊廟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Jimmu|qq=}} and the mausoleums of the previous three Emperors{{Efn2|In the case of {{ill|Jōkō|ja|上皇 (天皇退位特例法)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōkō|qq=}} Akihito, these three mausoleums are those of his great-grandfather, [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] at {{ill|Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|ja|伏見桃山陵|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Momoyama-ryō|qq=}}, his grandfather, [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] at [[:en:Musashi Imperial Graveyard|Tama no Misasagi]], and his father, [[:en:Hirohito|Emperor Shōwa]] at [[:en:Musashi Imperial Graveyard|Musashi Imperial Graveyard]].}}, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|qq=}} ([[:en:Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]]), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ([[:en:Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[:en:Shimogamo Shrine|Kamo Mizuo Shrine]]), [[:en:Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachimangū]], [[:en:Atsuta Shrine|Atsuta Shrine]], Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ([[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Shrine]]), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ([[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]]). On the occasion of Shihōhai in 2009 (Heisei 21), because of the advancing age of Emperor Akihito (the 125th Emperor) and the resulting simplification of the rites, the ceremony was performed at the {{ill|Gosho|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gosho|qq=}} within the Imperial Palace. == History == === From the founding period to the end of the Edo period === === Asuka period === The first documented reference to Shihōhai in Japan is in the [[:en:Nihon Shoki|Nihon Shoki]], under the entry for the first day of the eighth month of Empress {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|ja|皇極天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Empress Kōgyoku|qq=}}’s first year{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=90}}{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. It states that the Emperor “bowed to the four directions and looked up to heaven in prayer” while at Minabuchi, which is considered the earliest mention{{Sfnp|八束清貫|1957|p=11}}. Although the goal of Empress Kōgyoku’s Shihōhai at that time was [[:en:Rainmaking (ritual)|prayer for rain]], the fact that it was a direct Imperial worship and was called “Shihōhai” is believed to have some influential connection to the Shihōhai formalized during the Heian period{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=91-92}}{{Efn2|Empress Kōgyoku’s Chinese-style posthumous names “Kōgyoku” and, upon her reascension, “Saimei” are derived from Chinese classics, each term relating to “center” or the Big Dipper{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=113-114}}.}}. Furthermore, the Imperial mausoleums of the Asuka and [[:en:Fujiwara-kyō|Fujiwara-kyō]] periods were {{ill|eight-lobed tumuli|ja|八角墳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/eight-lobed tumuli|qq=}}, and even the Imperial throne (Takamikura) of the Daigokuden was octagonal. From this, it is believed that rites in Fujiwara-kyō symbolized control and peace over all lands in four or eight directions{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=276-280}}. Because of such characteristics, the possibility is raised that Shihōhai is linked to the Emperor’s supreme authority in worshipping the Northern Dipper, making it impossible to perform by proxy{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|p=337}}. === Heian period === Calamities such as [[:en:Disease|illness]], {{ill|epidemics|ja|疫病|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/epidemics|qq=}}, [[:en:Earthquake|earthquakes]], [[:en:Conflagration|fires]], and other {{ill|natural disasters|ja|天災|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/natural disasters|qq=}} were widely believed to be caused by the “{{ill|wrath of gods|ja|祟り|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/wrath of gods|qq=}},” with the gods responsible personified as [[:en:Oni|oni]] or {{ill|epidemic deities|ja|疫神|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/epidemic deities|qq=}}, which were greatly feared{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|斎藤英喜|2007|p=31}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|p=129}}. Because [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] had developed within the society of Heian aristocrats as a system of magical practices, numerous rites within the {{ill|Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制の神祇祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto of the Ritsuryō system|qq=}} included Onmyō elements{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=38}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=52}}. Various rites were performed, such as the {{ill|Ekishin-sai|ja|疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ekishin-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Chinka-sai|ja|鎮花祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinka-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Fūjin-sai|ja|風神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fūjin-sai|qq=}}, [[:en:Ōharae-shiki|Ōharae]], {{ill|Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|ja|宮城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai|qq=}}, {{ill|Bōke kasai-sai|ja|防解火災祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bōke kasai-sai|qq=}}, and {{ill|Keiwakusei-sai|ja|螢惑星祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keiwakusei-sai|qq=}}, to seal off Kyoto within ritual boundaries (dividing sacred and secular realms). Rites such as the “four corners and boundaries” ceremonies—{{ill|Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|ja|京城四隅疫神祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keijō shisui ekishin-sai|qq=}} (for the capital) and Miyagi shisui ekishin-sai (for the Imperial Palace)—were performed to pray for the peace of the realm{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=36}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|p=53}}. It is believed that the establishment of Shihōhai in the Heian period was influenced by Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]]’s adoption of the ancient Chinese imperial rite called {{ill|Jisa|ja|郊祀|1=Jiao Sacrifices|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jisa|13=User:Immanuelle/Jiao Sacrifices|qq=}}. This was the emperor’s ritual of offering sacrifices to heaven, which had been performed in ancient China and, among the kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, only in Baekje—where it was supported by the [[:en:Kudara no Konikishi clan|Baekje no Omi]]. Hence, it was carried out in Japan with their backing{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=138-154}}. The Shihōhai that is still performed today is said to have begun in the early Heian period, during the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Saga|Emperor Saga]] (early 9th century). It is believed that it became firmly established as a rite under Emperor [[:en:Emperor Uda|Emperor Uda]] (late 9th century). The oldest record of its performance is found in the [[:en:Kanpyō Gyoki|Uda Tennō Goki]] entry for the first day of the first month of the second year of Kanpyō (January 25, 890 in the Julian calendar). Emperor Uda wrote: “Our country is a land of the gods. Therefore, we should pay respect to the many gods, major and minor, in all four directions every morning. From now on, worship shall begin; never will it be neglected for a single day” (Uda Tennō Goki, entry for the 19th day of the tenth month, fourth year of Ninna). It is thought that these remarks reflect the creation of the daily worship known as “{{ill|Maichō Gohai|ja|毎朝御拝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maichō Gohai|qq=}},” which was established after Shihōhai on New Year’s morning had been instituted in Emperor Saga’s Kōnin era{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|p=136}}. === Azuchi–Momoyama period === Under [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]], there was a crackdown on [[:en:Onmyōji|Onmyōji]], driving practitioners of {{ill|incantations|ja|祈祷|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/incantations|qq=}} and [[:en:Divination|fortune-telling]] into the provinces and greatly diminishing their influence{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=33}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=44-48}}{{Sfnp|圭室文雄|2006|p=279}}. During the [[:en:Sengoku period|Sengoku period]] persecutions, even the main {{ill|Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado clan|lt=Tsuchimikado family|ja|土御門家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado family|qq=}} of the [[:en:Onmyōdō|Onmyōdō]] lost much of their scriptures, genealogies, and ritual implements—foremost among them the “great rites” ({{ill|Tai-san fukun-sai|ja|泰山府君祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tai-san fukun-sai|qq=}}) that centered on a specific [[:en:Altar|altar]]. Thus, the court had to borrow items from the [[:en:Yoshida Shrine|Yoshida Shrine]] in Kyoto to perform ground consecrations, and the Imperial Court rites took on a stronger Shinto character{{Sfnp|小池康寿|2015|p=34}}{{Sfnp|繁田信一|2005|pp=72-76}}{{Sfnp|林淳|2005|pp=75-77}}{{Sfnp|岡田荘司|2010|pp=136-137}}. Meanwhile, with official permission from the Edo Shogunate, {{ill|Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|ja|土御門泰福|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado Yasutomi|qq=}} introduced Shinto influences into Onmyōdō and developed “Tensha Shintō” under the impact of {{ill|Torigoe Shintō|ja|垂加神道|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Torigoe Shintō|qq=}}{{Sfnp|木場明志|1982|pp=65-66}}. Other Imperial worship rites could sometimes be performed by proxy, such as by the {{ill|Sesshō and Kampaku|ja|摂関|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sesshō and Kampaku|qq=}} or the {{ill|Jingi-haku|ja|神祇伯|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jingi-haku|qq=}}, but Shihōhai never was. Since the Emperor’s own guardian star and his parents (or ancestors) were worshipped, the ritual could not be substituted. In his 18th-century text ''{{ill|Iesetsu ryakuki|ja|家説略記|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iesetsu ryakuki|qq=}}'', {{ill|Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|ja|白川雅喬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa Yukitada (Jakugyō)|qq=}} noted that Shihōhai is a ceremony for worshipping the guardian star and royal mausoleums; he thus argued that it was not a Shinto rite (“非神祭”), suggesting it may have originated under the influence of [[:en:Taoism|Taoism]] or Onmyōdō{{Sfnp|村和明|2013|pp=254-260、275-276}}. Following the example of the Emperor, [[:en:Nobility|nobles]] and commoners alike once performed Shihōhai to pray for abundant harvests and good health for the coming year{{Efn2|''Eke shidai'' contains mention of “Sekkan Shihōhai” and “Ceremony for the common subjects,” though citations are needed.}}. Over the course of time, however, it was eventually preserved only as an Imperial Court ritual{{Efn2|Nevertheless, records suggest that some [[:en:Kuge|Kuge]] families, such as the [[:en:Five regent houses|Five regent houses]], performed Shihōhai even in the Edo period. For instance, in the diary “''Kaneka-kō ki''” by [[:en:Ichijō Kaneka|Ichijō Kaneka]], who served as {{ill|Kampaku|ja|関白|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kampaku|qq=}} in the third year of Genbun (1738), it is recorded that, unlike the Emperor’s Shihōhai with three seats, his Shihōhai lacked three seats and replaced Imperial mausoleums with the mausoleums and shrines related to the [[:en:Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara clan]] and Onmyōdō. Citations are needed.}}. Although it was interrupted by the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] in the late 15th century, Shihōhai was restored in the seventh year of [[:en:Civilization|Bunmei (Japanese era)]] (1475) during the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado|Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado]] and continued in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}} in the [[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] up through the reign of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Kōmei|Emperor Kōmei]] in the late 19th century. === Ceremony before the Meiji period === On January 1, at the hour of the Tiger (around 4 a.m.), the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor]] donned the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayahashidono|qq=}} of the {{ill|Imperial Palace|ja|御所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|qq=}} and then appeared in the eastern courtyard of the {{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}}. In that courtyard, three seats were prepared in advance: the “Jokusei-gohai-gōza” (Guardian Star Worship Seat), the “Shihō-gohai-gōza” (Four Directions Worship Seat), and the “Sanryō-gohai-gōza” (Imperial Mausoleum Worship Seat). First, the Emperor sat on the Jokusei-gohai-gōza and worshipped the Emperor’s guardian star ({{ill|Zokushō|ja|属星|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zokushō|qq=}}){{Efn2|A “guardian star” is one of the stars of the [[:en:Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] believed to govern the destiny of a person according to their birth year: the star is Dūbei (貪狼星) for the Year of the Rat, Merak (巨門星) for the Ox and Boar, Phecda (禄存星) for the Tiger and Dog, Megrez (文曲星) for the Hare and Rooster, Alioth (廉貞星) for the Dragon and Monkey, Mizar (武曲星) for the Snake and Goat, and Alkaid (破軍星) for the Horse.{{Cite Kotobank|属星|encyclopedia=精選版 日本国語大辞典（小学館）|accessdate=2023-12-14}}}}. Next, he moved to the Shihō-gohai-gōza to worship the gods and spirits of heaven and earth in the four directions. Lastly, he moved to the Sanryō-gohai-gōza to worship the tombs of his parents (unless they were still living) and so forth. At each seat, he prayed for the peace of the realm and for the prolongation of the Imperial line. In the Edo period, after worshipping the guardian star, the Emperor also worshipped the {{ill|Naishidokoro|ja|内侍所|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishidokoro|qq=}} and [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]] from the Jokusei-gohai-gōza, and before worshipping the tombs of his parents, he worshipped the mausoleums of past Emperors (specific targets varied depending on the period) from the Sanryō-gohai-gōza. Regarding worship at Ise Grand Shrine, records in the diary “''Hanazono Tennō Nikki''” for the second year of Gen’ō (1320) indicate that it was customary in the {{ill|Nyoin|ja|院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nyoin|qq=}} Shihōhai since the time of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Fukakusa|Emperor Go-Fukakusa]], and it is thought that this was later adopted for the Emperor’s Shihōhai. During worship, the Emperor recited a unique chant (incantation). According to ''{{ill|Naidairi Gishiki|ja|内裏儀式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naidairi Gishiki|qq=}}'' and ''{{ill|Eke Shidai|ja|江家次第|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eke Shidai|qq=}}'', it went as follows: {{Squote| {{ruby|賊寇之中過度我身|ぞくこうしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒魔之中過度我身|どくましちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毒氣之中過度我身|どくけしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|毀厄之中過度我身|きやくしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五危六害之中過度我身|ごきろくがいしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|五兵六舌之中過度我身|ごへいろくぜつしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|厭魅之中過度我身|えんみしちゅうかどがしん}}
{{ruby|萬病除癒|まんびょうじょゆ}}
{{ruby|所欲随心|しょよくずいしん}}
{{ruby|急々如律令|きゅうきゅうにょりつりょう}} }} Some sources write “五厄” (five calamities) instead of “五危” (five dangers). Prior to the Meiji era, the ritual implements for the New Year’s Day Shihōhai included a “'''Daisō-byōbu'''” (大宋御屏風). “Daisō” refers to the Chinese Liu Song dynasty, and it is viewed as an item passed down from the ancient Chinese “Bright Hall Sacrifice” ({{ill|Ming tang sacrifice|ja|明堂祭祀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ming tang sacrifice|qq=}}) to Japan through the Southern dynasties, signifying that New Year’s Shihōhai is connected to the worship of heaven and earth by ancient Chinese emperors. The Emperor’s ceremonial robe of yellow—{{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}}—is interpreted as expressing the central soil color “yellow” of the “{{ill|Yueling|ja|月令|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yueling|qq=}}” ideology, further indicating its relation to ancient Chinese imperial rites{{Sfnp|石野浩司|2011|pp=149-154}}. According to ''Naidairi Gishiki'' and ''Saigū-ki'' (also known as ''Sai no Miya-ki''), on New Year’s Day before dawn, at the hour of the Ox (around 2 a.m.), four panels of screens were set in the eastern courtyard, an oil lamp was placed in front of the seat where the guardian star was worshipped, and incense and flowers were offered on whitewood tables before each seat. Starting from the hour of the Tiger (about 3 a.m.), the Emperor performed: # Worship of the guardian star (Zokushō), # Worship of the four directions of heaven and earth, # Worship of two tombs (that of his father and mother), if applicable{{Sfnp|渡辺瑞穂子|2020|pp=79-80}}. === After the Meiji period === After the Meiji Restoration, under the influence of [[:en:Kokugaku|Kokugaku]], elements considered to be derived from [[:en:Taoism|Taoism]] (such as worshipping the [[:en:Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] guardian star and chanting “kyūkyū nyo ritsuryō”) were removed, and Shihōhai was reframed as a [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] ceremony. It became a state observance called “Shihōsetsu,” one of the four major official holidays. ;Ceremony after the Meiji period A temporary shelter is set up beforehand in the southern courtyard of the Shinka-den, which is part of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] of the Imperial Palace, and inside it, a reed mat is laid, two pairs of screens are placed around it, and a seat is arranged with two lamps offered. At 5:30 a.m. on January 1, the Emperor dresses in the {{ill|Kōrozen no gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōrozen no gohō|qq=}} in the {{ill|Ayahashidono|ja|綾綺殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayahashidono|qq=}} and proceeds, led by the {{ill|Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|ja|掌典長|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōtenchō (Chief of Ceremonies)|qq=}}, to the south courtyard of the Shinka-den. Taking his seat there, he first worships toward the two shrines of the [[:en:Ise Shrine|Ise Grand Shrine]]—the {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt=Kōtaijingū|ja|皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtaijingū|qq=}} and the {{ill|Tōyuke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōyuke Daijingū|qq=}}—and then toward the other deities of the four directions. At this time, the Emperor worships the following gods and Imperial mausoleums in turn: Ise Grand Shrine, {{ill|Kami|lt=Kami|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|qq=}}, the mausoleum of [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] and those of the previous three Emperors, {{ill|Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国一宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinomiya of Musashi Province|qq=}} ([[:en:Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]]), Ichinomiya of Yamashiro Province ([[:en:Kamigamo Shrine|Kamo Wakeikazuchi Shrine]] and [[:en:Shimogamo Shrine|Kamo Mizuo Shrine]]), [[:en:Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachimangū]], [[:en:Atsuta Shrine|Atsuta Shrine]], Ichinomiya of Hitachi Province ([[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Shrine]]), and Ichinomiya of Shimōsa Province ([[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]]). After concluding Shihōhai, the Emperor proceeds to worship at each of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] (the Kashiko-dokoro, the Kōrei-den, and the Shin-den). If the Emperor cannot personally perform Shihōhai for some reason, custom dictates that no proxy will be appointed, in accordance with historical practice. On New Year’s Day of Shōwa 20 (1945), during World War II, an air-raid alarm sounded for a raid by {{ill|B-29 bombers|ja|B29爆撃機|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/B-29 bombers|qq=}}. Nevertheless, Emperor [[:en:Hirohito|Emperor Shōwa]] carried out Shihōhai in front of the {{ill|O-bunko|ja|御文庫|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/O-bunko|qq=}} (the Imperial archives), which had been set up as an air-raid shelter{{Sfnp|藤田尚徳|2015|pp=9-11}}. == Notes == === Annotations === {{Notelist2}} === References === {{Reflist|20em}} == Bibliography == ;Books * {{Cite book|和書|author=松山能夫|title=明治維新神道百年史|publisher=神道文化会|date=1966-4|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=繁田信一|title=平安貴族と陰陽師|publisher=[[吉川弘文館]]|date=2005-05|isbn=9784642079426|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=林淳|title=近世陰陽道の研究|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2005-12|isbn=4642034072|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=圭室文雄|title=日本人の宗教と庶民信仰|publisher=吉川弘文館|date=2006-3|isbn=9784642013673|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=斎藤英喜|title=陰陽道の神々|publisher=佛教大学教育部思文閣出版|date=2007-10|isbn=9784784213665|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田荘司|title=日本神道史|publisher= 吉川弘文館|date=2010-06|isbn=9784642080385|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=石野浩司|title=石灰壇「毎朝御拝」の史的研究|publisher=皇學館大学出版部|date=2011-02|isbn=9784876441693|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=村和明|title=近世の朝廷制度と朝幕関係|publisher=東京大学出版会|date=2013-02|isbn=9784130262330|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=藤田尚徳|title=侍従長の回想|publisher=[[講談社]]|series=[[講談社学術文庫]]|date=2015-03|isbn=9784062922845|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=小池康寿|title=日本人なら知っておきたい正しい家相の本|publisher=[[プレジデント社]]|date=2015-11|isbn=9784833421492|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=渡辺瑞穂子|title=元旦四方拝の研究|publisher=啓文社書房|date=2020-01|isbn=9784899920625|ref=harv}} * {{Cite book|和書|author=[[八束清貫]]|title=皇室と神宮|publisher=[[神宮司廳教導部]]|date=1957-06|ref=harv}} ;Articles *{{Cite journal|和書|author=木場明志|title=近世土御門家の陰陽師支配と配下陰陽師|journal=大谷学報|ISSN=02876027|publisher=大谷学会|date=1982-12|volume=62|issue=3|pages=54-67|naid=120005768577|url=http://id.nii.ac.jp/1374/00001885/|ref=harv}} ;Dictionaries *Heibonsha (ed.). “Shihōhai” entry in ''Shintō Daijiten'' (Vol. 2). Heibonsha, 1941, p. 99. == See also == *[[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]] *[[:en:Kyoto Imperial Palace|Kyoto Imperial Palace]] *{{ill|Seiryō-den|ja|清涼殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiryō-den|qq=}} *{{ill|Oni no Ma|ja|鬼の間|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oni no Ma|qq=}} *[[:en:Sarugatsuji|Saru-ga-tsuji]] {{Shinto-stub}} {{translated page|ja|四方拝|version=104519723|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:New Year]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Japanese groupings of four]] [[Category:New Year kigo]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Shihohai]][[Category:qq]] }} [[ja:四方拝]] [[sn:Shihohai]] [[Category:新春の季語]] [[Category:日本の名数4]]
